陆峥走到沈予安身旁，视线扫过对方肩背，最后落到攥紧瓶身的指尖。周遭器械运转的声响嘈杂，他压低音量说话，声音刚好可以传到沈予安耳朵里。
“肩膀难受。”
沈予安抬眼，视线对上陆峥，轻轻晃动脑袋。
“不耽误手上的活。”
陆峥的目光停留在左肩衣物覆盖的位置，布料之下就是旧伤的轮廓。他没有继续追问，身体侧转半步，挡在沈予安身前，把作业区涌过来的穿堂风拦在自己背后。
沈予安的视线短暂停留在陆峥宽厚的肩膀，随即移回被灯光铺满的勘验现场。
“物证提取接近收尾，遗体可以运回检验科。死者属于成年男性，骨骼不存在粉碎外力损伤，致命伤不在体表。确切死因、死亡时间、药物残留全部要等解剖送检才能得出结论。”
“你跟着转运车回局里。天亮之前交初检报告就行，不用硬赶速度。”陆峥开口，给沈予安划定的时间窗口，和队内其余人员连夜加急的要求拉开差距。
沈予安点头应答。
技术组组长捧着平板快步靠近，屏幕铺满园区监控点位分布图和轨迹推演图纸。
“陆队，园区四十六处固定监控，十二个巡更抓拍点位，全部避开雕塑夹层的作案位置。嫌疑人对整片园区盲区的掌握程度，等同于内部拿到完整施工规划。”
手指滑动平板页面，放出近七天夜间的监控录像片段。空旷园区里游客、保安的行动轨迹清晰，那名穿黑色连帽卫衣的男子，入场和离场两段完整轨迹全部消失，仿佛凭空出现，又消融进绿化带阴影。
“城郊周边天网、沿街商铺监控已经全部调取完成，组员正在逐帧拆解录像。嫌疑人全程走绿化带、背光步道、墙体阴影，避开全部主干道镜头，拿不到正面人脸，也没有清晰体态特写。”
陆峥看向平板屏幕上密密麻麻的盲区标记。
“锁定排查窗口，凌晨一点到四点，筛查一周之内所有城郊进出园区的步行人员，重点挑单人行进、步速稳定，不在沿途逗留观望的目标。联系网安部门，回溯La Rose Éternelle暗网IP跳转记录，交叉比对安市半个月之内异常网络访问记录。实体物证和网络线索两条线同步推进。”
技术组组长接下指令转身离开。
时间走到深夜十一点。密封尸箱被抬上刑侦转运车辆，证物贴好防伪封条分批送往物证室与检验科。外勤留下两个人通宵驻守保护现场，其余人员拆除多余警戒设施。喧闹的作业动静慢慢消散，广场重新变得空旷，探照灯依旧打在巨型石雕上，石缝之间还留着零星玫瑰花瓣碎屑。
队员陆续登车，汽车引擎低沉轰鸣。
陆峥看向身侧的沈予安。
“你先上车。”
沈予安迈步走向法医转运车，刚踏出一步，小臂被轻轻拦停。陆峥指尖碰到制服衣袖，没有直接接触皮肤。
“坐到后座，找地方靠一靠，不要压左肩。”
沈予安侧过头，灯光描出下颌线条。
“明白。”
他拉开车门坐进车里，车门闭合隔开外面的夜色。陆峥站在原地，目送车辆亮起车灯驶离园区，车尾光点转过道路拐角彻底看不见，才收回目光。
巨型雕塑立在黑暗当中，仪式化的藏尸现场留在石材夹层。接连两起仪式凶案，作案手法稳定，布局周密，反侦察手段成熟。凶手不追求频繁作案，每一次行凶都是一套完整流程复刻，更像向背后的组织递交成果。
陆峥对着剩下的队员出声。
“所有人返程。”
三辆警车依次发动，车灯划破郊外黑暗，顺着柏油公路驶离雕塑公园。车厢内部气氛压抑，没有人闲聊，队员低头整理现场采集到的笔记，平板屏幕的微光映在一张张脸上。
回到市局大楼已是午夜。整栋主楼大半楼层灯光熄灭，只有刑侦支队、法医检验科、网安办公室还灯火通明。走廊地砖反射天花板白光，脚步声响在空旷过道来回回荡。
沈予安下车直接走进法医检验科，穿戴全套解剖防护装备进入解剖室。金属解剖台冷硬冰凉，尸箱被推送到位，器械碰撞发出细碎金属响动。解剖室外的办公区，陆峥站在玻璃窗外面，隔着一层玻璃看向室内忙碌的身影，没有推门进去打扰，靠在墙面翻看现场拷贝回来的监控素材。
监控录像一帧帧向前滚动，屏幕里面只有公园空旷步道、摇曳的灌木，找不到嫌疑人的蛛丝马迹。
几组走访笔录文档同步传到平板。公园保洁、保安、物业工作人员的口供反复比对，能够确定的线索，只有三天凌晨保安撞见的那道黑色人影。其余信息全部是无效碎片。
支队办公室不断传来键盘敲击声，网安小组调取海量网络日志，筛选暗网访问痕迹。一条条IP地址不断弹出屏幕，大部分属于无效跳板，真实源头被层层代理掩盖。
一名年轻警员抱着一摞打印好的笔录文件走过来，把纸张放到陆峥手边的桌面。
“陆队，园区内部人员全部排查完毕，在岗职工不存在医学解剖相关从业经历，近半年也没有外来人员应聘短期岗位。”
陆峥翻动纸质笔录，纸上密密麻麻记录问询内容。
“扩大范围，排查近一年从本市离职的解剖、外科相关从业人员，同时比对有过境外旅居记录人员名单。不要局限在本市常住人口库。”
警员记下指令转身离开。
检验科解剖室的灯光持续亮着。解剖工作消耗大量时间，解剖器械有条不紊运作，沈予安专注处理遗体，记录下每一处刀口、骨骼状态，提取血液、组织样本送去化验室。左肩的酸胀持续存在，他调整站姿，把身体重量更多分摊到右腿，手上动作节奏没有半点打乱。
窗外天色一点点由墨黑转为灰蓝，天边泛起极淡的晨光。城市还没有完全苏醒，街道车流稀疏。
玻璃隔断外面，陆峥依旧守在走廊，桌上堆起厚厚一叠纸质卷宗，平板屏幕停留在还未筛查完毕的监控画面。他偶尔抬眼望向解剖室内部，视线落向那个忙碌的背影，再低下头继续翻阅案卷。
检验科房门推开，沈予安走出来，脱去外层防护服，口罩摘下来握在手里，额角沾着一层薄汗。他手里拿着几页纸质初检报告，纸张上面写满手写勘验记录。
“死者男性，年龄三十六至三十八岁。真正致命损伤在胸腔内部，脏器遭锐器贯穿。体表分割属于死后完成，刀口全部对应专业解剖入刀角度。胃内容物检测结果可以锁定死亡时间，案发就在三天前凌晨两点前后。身体采样已经送去化验室，药物、毒物报告还需要等待。”
沈予安把报告递过去。陆峥伸手接过纸张，指尖碰到纸面，目光扫过报告上面一行行勘验结论。
“花瓣、石材缝隙样本呢。”
“物证室接手，正在做微量物质比对，看能不能追踪花瓣采购来源。”
陆峥合上报告，目光落在沈予安脸上。通宵高强度工作过后，对方眼底浮起淡淡的疲惫。
“隔壁休息室有床，你过去躺一会。化验室结果出来我让人通知你。”
沈予安没有推辞，接过陆峥递过来的一次性水杯，走向走廊尽头休息室。门板闭合，隔绝外面办公室嘈杂声响。
支队办公区依旧高速运转。监控筛查小组几十台显示器同时播放录像片段，警员眼睛盯着屏幕，反复回看公园周边各个路口画面。海量视频素材堆在服务器硬盘，四天的排查周期就此拉开。大量人力物力投入线索挖掘，所有人的调查方向全部朝外，把全部怀疑投向潜藏在城市之外的神秘组织。
清晨六点半，天光漫过安市连片的楼宇，薄薄的晨雾压在城市低空，冲淡了深夜的寒意。街头早班车流缓缓涌动，细碎的鸣响隔着双层玻璃窗渗入刑侦办公室，搅碎整夜凝固的沉寂。
刑侦支队整层办公室依旧亮着白昼灯光。成排监控屏幕蓝光闪烁，铺满墙面，数十名警员紧盯画面，指尖不停敲击键盘，全程沉浸在海量视频筛查工作里，紧绷的氛围没有半分松弛。
为期四天的全域摸排，正式全面铺开。
陆峥端坐工位，指腹轻控鼠标，反复拖拽监控进度条，一寸寸复盘雕塑公园周边凌晨一点至四点的空白时段画面。桌面层层叠叠摊开死者档案、现场测绘图纸、全员问询笔录，纸张边缘被反复翻看摩挲，微微卷起。
死者身份信息已经完全核实落地。
赵强，三十八岁，安市本地无业人员，留有三次小额盗窃、聚众滋事案底。常年辗转城郊出租屋，无固定居所，无稳定社交圈，亲属疏离，往来人员杂乱且无规律。
系统筛查的所有关联线索，干净得反常。
此人没有任何外科、解剖、医护从业履历，无花艺研习记录，无审美艺术相关从业或兴趣备案，设备浏览记录里从未出现过境外暗网入口。他和仪式化凶案需要的专业素养、审美认知、反侦察能力，没有半点匹配之处。
他只是一个随机筛选的牺牲品，无恩怨纠葛，无私人仇怨，只是凶手为完成组织仪轨，随手挑选的适配载体。
陆峥视线落在屏幕里空旷的公园步道画面，眉骨线条压得冷硬。
随机献祭、规整仪式、零遗留私怨、极致周密的布局。
凶手的目标从来不是某一个人，是一场持续、规律、可复刻的犯罪展演。
他抬手点开队内工作群，指尖快速敲击键盘，下发新一轮排查指令，措辞精准利落，没有一句多余赘述。
“全员扩大筛查半径至八公里。重点排查近一周凌晨独居夜行人员、无出行轨迹记录人员、反复出现在城郊空白路段的陌生面孔。技术组交叉比对两起命案周边所有废弃监控盲区，汇总重叠点位。走访组二次回访园区所有在岗人员，逐人核对夜间异常细节。”
指令一键发送，办公区各组队员同步接收，即刻推进工作，分工衔接毫无滞涩。
走廊尽头的休息室房门闭合严实。
室内遮光帘完全拉合，隔绝了外界晨光与声响，密闭空间里光线昏暗静谧。
沈予安平躺于折叠休息床上，四肢舒展，脊背贴合床板，双目轻阖。
表层姿态是彻底放松休憩的模样，完美贴合通宵工作后疲惫休眠的状态。
但他没有入睡。
精神分裂带来的认知割裂感，在无人观测的独处空间里彻底挣脱伪装桎梏。细碎且扭曲的幻听在耳膜深处层层堆叠，杂乱的低语、细碎的摩挲声、模糊的仪式念响环绕耳畔，常人无法承受的感官错乱，是他常年独处的常态。
双向情感障碍的低温低谷状态彻底笼罩身心。
通体寒凉麻木，情绪剥离殆尽，疲惫，倦怠，办案后的紧绷松弛這些都沒有只剩一片死寂的漠然。
他清晰记得昨夜整场勘验、所有对话、动作细节。
记得陆峥侧身替他遮挡穿堂风的站位，记得对方刻意放宽的报告时限，记得紧盯他肩伤的视线，记得全程寸步不离的留守看护。...沈予安微微一笑“這真是令人感動啊陸警官”沈予安的指尖在床沿边缘轻轻敲了两下，节奏均匀，像在默数什么。
幻听的杂音慢慢退潮，残留的尾音贴着耳膜打转，不疼，只是吵。他睁开眼，瞳孔在昏暗光线里收缩一瞬，随即恢复正常焦距。
天花板的白色水渍纹路固定在同一个位置，他数过，七块。
翻身坐起，动作流畅，没有通宵沉睡后该有的滞涩。他拉过椅背上搭着的制服外套穿上，扣好最后一颗纽扣，抬手理平领口褶皱。镜子里映出一张没什么表情的脸，眼底干净，看不出任何端倪。
推门出去的时候，走廊里的白炽灯光线刺得人眯眼。
办公区依旧人声鼎沸。有人抱着一摞打印纸快步穿过过道，有人对着电话反复核对监控时间码，白板上贴满了嫌疑人模拟画像、路口方位图、死者社会关系网状图，红笔标注的线索连线密密麻麻。
陆峥站在白板前，手里捏着一支黑色记号笔，正在两起命案的案发地点之间画虚线。衬衫袖口卷到小臂，腕骨线条硬挺，指节上沾了一点白板笔的墨渍。
听见脚步声，他侧过头。
"醒了？"
沈予安走过去，目光扫过白板上的轨迹图，声音带着刚醒后的一丝低哑，恰到好处。"几点了。"
"九点四十。"陆峥把笔帽扣上，转身从桌上拎过一个塑料袋递过来，"食堂带的豆浆和包子，还热着。"
袋子是温的，隔着薄塑料膜能摸到温度。沈予安接过来，指尖擦过对方的指节，停留不到半秒，自然得像无意。
"谢谢陆队。"
他拉开旁边的椅子坐下，拆开豆浆吸管，动作不快不慢。陆峥重新转回去面对白板，指尖点在两处案发现场的连线上。
"技术组刚出结果。两起命案的抛尸点，刚好分布在环城线的东西两端，中间直线距离十七公里。凶手选点不是随机的，是沿着同一条路线踩过的。"
沈予安咬了一口包子，咀嚼的速度平稳，视线跟着陆峥的指尖移动。
"监控盲区的重叠区域呢。"
"找到了。"陆峥在白板角落圈出一个不规则色块，"城西旧机床厂，废弃六年，围墙塌了两段，周围三百米没有一个民用监控。天网也覆盖不到。"
他顿了一下，声音压低半度。"如果两起案子是同一个人做的，这里大概率是中转点。"
沈予安放下豆浆杯，手指在杯壁上轻轻摩挲。
旧机床厂。
他当然知道那个地方。三天前凌晨四点十七分，他把最后一瓣玫瑰花瓣从外套口袋里抖出来，落在机床铁台面上的时候，东边的天刚泛起灰。清理完所有痕迹，他从围墙北端的缺口翻出去，拐进一条早市必经的小巷，混在第一批进货的摊贩中间走了两个街区，才拦了一辆夜班出租。
全程没有抬头。
"要不要现在过去看。"他开口，语气是标准的法医问询口吻，冷静，专业，不带多余情绪。
陆峥摇头。"外勤已经先过去了，封锁现场，等你过去出勘验结果。"
他说的是"等你"，不是"等你们"。
办公区旁边经过的两个队员听见了，脚步没停，表情也没变。这种话从陆峥嘴里说出来，早就和"注意安全"一样平常。
沈予安站起身，把剩下的半个包子塞进纸袋，揉成一团扔进垃圾桶。
旧机床厂比想象中破得彻底。
围墙外围爬满了枯死的爬山虎，枝桠像干裂的血管贴在水泥面上。正门的铁栅门被人撬过，锁扣歪在一边，挂着锈迹斑斑的铁链。里面三栋厂房排成凹字形，屋顶塌了两处长条，阳光从破洞里斜插进来，在地面投下斑驳的光斑。
空气里弥漫着铁锈、潮土和某种腐败植物混合的气味。
外勤已经拉好了警戒线，两个穿制服的警员守在门口，见到陆峥过来，主动掀开警戒带。
"陆队，里面靠东头那间厂房，地上有残留花瓣，还有拖拽痕迹。其余地方暂时没发现异常。"
陆峥点头，侧身让出位置。"沈法医先看。"
沈予安蹲下身，从勘验包里取出手套戴上。指尖碰到地面的瞬间，他的视线开始系统性地扫过每一寸地面——从门槛到墙角，从机床底座到排水渠边缘。
花瓣残片被外勤单独装在证物袋里，他接过来举到光线下看了一眼。
和雕塑公园里的品种一模一样，卡罗拉白玫瑰，花瓣边缘修剪过，切口整齐。
他把证物袋递回给记录员，声音平稳。"拖拽痕迹从厂房中央延伸到东墙根，地面有浅色擦蹭，应该是布料或者塑料布留下的。花瓣散落范围集中在拖痕两侧半米内，符合搬运过程中意外掉落。"
站起身，他绕着厂房走了一圈。
墙角有半个模糊的鞋印，被灰尘盖了大半。他蹲下去，用比例尺贴在旁边，让记录员拍照。鞋印四十一码，运动鞋纹路，后跟磨损偏外侧。
"和雕塑公园外围提取到的鞋印比对过吗。"他问。
技术组的人翻了一下平板。"纹路不同，那双鞋印是四十三码，工装靴。"
沈予安"嗯"了一声，没再说话。
他当然知道纹路不同。机床厂这里留下的鞋印，是他故意穿另一双鞋踩的。搬运过程中换鞋，是仪轨里最基础的反侦察步骤。
陆峥站在厂房门口，双臂抱在胸前，目光一直跟着他转。
沈予安直起腰的时候，左肩微微偏了一下，幅度很小，像是长时间蹲姿引起的正常酸僵。他抬手活动了一下肩颈，指节按在肩窝的位置，轻轻揉了两下。
下一秒，陆峥的声音从身后传过来。
"蹲太久了？"
"还行。"沈予安回头，表情平淡。
陆峥走过来，目光在他左肩停了一秒，随即移开，转向技术组。"外围搜完没有。"
"搜完了，围墙缺口那边有半个指纹，已经提取了。另外在厂后面的垃圾堆里找到一个一次性餐盒，里面有剩饭，还有半瓶矿泉水，不确定是不是嫌疑人留下的。"
"送检。"陆峥说。
从机床厂出来已经过了正午。
日头毒，柏油路面被晒得发软，空气里飘着汽车尾气的热浪。外勤队员留在现场继续搜证，陆峥和沈予安驱车回市局。
车里开着空调，冷气从出风口喷出来，吹得人手臂发凉。
沈予安靠在副驾座椅上，侧头看窗外。街景飞速后退，行道树的影子在他脸上一帧帧划过。
陆峥单手握着方向盘，另一只手肘搭在车窗沿，沉默了一会儿，忽然开口。
"昨晚解剖到几点。"
"三点多。"
"为什么不叫我。"
沈予安偏过脸，看了他一眼。"陆队又不用熬通宵。"
这句话答得轻巧，带着一点恰到好处的生分，又不显得疏远。像一个下属对上级的体谅，分寸拿捏得刚好。
陆峥的喉结动了一下，没再接话。
车载电台突然响了，技术组的声音带着电流杂音传出来。"陆队，花瓣比对结果出来了。两起案子用的白玫瑰，都是从城南同一家鲜切花批发市场拿的货，品种和批次完全一致。"
"批发市场有没有监控。"
"有，但那片区域监控老化，像素极低，人脸根本看不清。我们正在调取一周前的出货记录，看看有没有大单采购白玫瑰的客户。"
"继续。"
电台断了。
车里重新安静下来。沈予安收回视线，重新看向窗外。他的手指在膝盖上轻轻敲了两下，节奏和早上在休息室里敲床沿的频率一模一样。
城南批发市场。
他知道那家市场。买花那天是凌晨五点，市场刚开门，批发商还在卸货，他戴了口罩和鸭舌帽，现金付的账，买了两扎白玫瑰，装在黑色塑料袋里。整个过程不到四分钟，没和任何人多说话。
监控就算调出来，也只会拍到一个模糊的口罩身影。
车驶进市局大院，停稳。陆峥拔了钥匙，转头看他。
"下午没你什么事了，回办公室补一觉。化验报告出来我让人送你桌上。"
沈予安解安全带的动作顿了半拍，随即点头。"好。"
他推开车门，脚刚踩到地面，又被陆峥叫住。
"沈予安。"
他回头。
陆峥坐在驾驶座上，手还搭在方向盘上，日光从他背后照过来，五官轮廓嵌在逆光里，看不太清表情。
"肩膀的药，记得换。"
沈予安站在车外，垂在身侧的手指几不可察地蜷了一下。
"知道。"
他转身往大楼里走，背影笔直，步速平稳。
陆峥坐在车里，看着那个背影消失在大门玻璃后面，才发动车子，把车开进地下车库。
办公室里，监控筛查还在继续。白板上的线索图又多了几条红色连线，花瓣来源、机床厂中转点、城西监控盲区，三个点被圈在一起，形成一个模糊的三角形。
所有人都在朝这个三角形靠近。
没有人想到，三角形的中心，就坐在三楼法医办公室的椅子上，正对着窗外发了两秒钟的呆，然后伸手拉开抽屉，拿出一份新的尸检记录表，开始提笔填写。
笔尖落在纸上，字迹工整，力道均匀。
他写得很专注，像在完成一件必须做到完美的作品。
en: Cold floodlights fixed on the granite of the sculpture plaza, cutting through the dense night and revealing every ridge in the stone. Evidence packaging continued. Petal fragments and dust from the crevices went into clear bags, each marked with its collection point and time, then arranged on a metal trolley. Field officers set up a third cordon, preserving a three-meter core around the sculpture against any outside contact.
Wind passed through the trees and swept the plaza with the chill of earth and vegetation.

Shen Yu’an stepped outside the barrier, holding the unopened bottle of water. His back was straight, eyes on the examination. Prolonged standing sent an ache from the old wound through his shoulder and neck. His uniform concealed the discomfort. Only his fingers tightening around the bottle betrayed the strain.

Lu Zheng signed the temporary scene report and handed the board to an officer. Removing his earpiece, he crossed through the busy teams toward the barrier. Technicians crouched over footprints, field officers adjusted recording equipment, and a liaison exchanged data with the laboratory. No one watched where the team leader went.
He stopped beside Shen Yu’an. His gaze passed over the shoulders and back, then settled on the fingers gripping the bottle. Amid the equipment noise, he spoke just loudly enough to be heard.
“Your shoulder hurts.”
Shen Yu’an looked at him and gave a small shake of his head.
“It won’t interfere with the work.”

Lu Zheng’s eyes rested where the clothing covered the wound. He did not press the question. Instead, he turned half a step in front of Shen Yu’an, taking the draft from the working area against his own back.
Shen Yu’an’s gaze paused briefly on the broad shoulders, then returned to the floodlit scene.

“Evidence recovery is nearly finished. The body can go back to the laboratory. An adult male, no comminuted trauma to the bones. The fatal injury isn’t on the surface. Cause and time of death, and any drug residue, will need the autopsy and tests.”
“Go back with the transport vehicle. A preliminary report before daylight is enough. Don’t rush it.” Lu Zheng allowed him a wider window than the urgent overnight schedule assigned to everyone else.
Shen Yu’an nodded.
The technical team leader approached quickly with a tablet displaying camera positions and reconstructed routes through the park.

“Team Leader Lu, none of the forty-six fixed cameras or twelve patrol capture points covers the crime location within the sculpture. The suspect knows the blind spots as well as someone with the full construction plans.”

He swiped to night footage from the previous week. Visitors and guards moved clearly through the empty grounds, but the man in a black hooded sweatshirt had no complete entry or exit trail. He seemed to appear from nowhere and dissolve into the planting beds.

“We’ve obtained the surrounding public-security footage and shop cameras. Officers are going through it frame by frame. He stayed in planted areas, unlit paths and wall shadows, avoiding every main-route camera. No frontal face image or clear close view of his build.”
Lu Zheng studied the dense marks indicating blind spots.

“Set the window from one to four in the morning. Check everyone entering or leaving on foot over the past week. Prioritize solitary people walking steadily without stopping to look around. Contact cybercrime. Trace the IP hops for La Rose Éternelle and cross-check unusual network access in An’an over the past half-month. Physical evidence and online leads move together.”
The team leader took the orders and left.

By eleven, the sealed body container was loaded into a transport vehicle. Tamper-evident seals were applied to evidence going in batches to storage and the laboratory. Two field officers remained to guard the scene overnight; the rest dismantled unnecessary barriers. The noise subsided and the plaza emptied. Floodlights still illuminated the giant stone sculpture, with a few rose-petal fragments left in its seams.
Officers boarded the vehicles. Engines rumbled.
Lu Zheng looked at Shen Yu’an.
“Go ahead.”
Shen Yu’an started toward the forensic vehicle. After one step, a light touch stopped his forearm. Lu Zheng’s fingers touched the uniform sleeve, not his skin.
“Take the back seat. Lean against something. Don’t press on the left shoulder.”
Shen Yu’an turned, light outlining his jaw.
“Understood.”
He opened the door and got in. When it closed, the night outside was shut away. Lu Zheng watched the vehicle leave, following its rear lights until they disappeared around the bend.

The giant sculpture stood in darkness, the ritualized crime concealed within its stone structure. Two successive ritual cases, steady methods, careful planning and practiced evasion. The killer was not trying to offend frequently. Each act repeated a complete process, almost as if submitting finished work to the organization behind him.
Lu Zheng addressed the remaining officers.
“Everyone back.”
Three police vehicles started in sequence and followed the asphalt road away from the park. No one chatted. Officers organized notes in the subdued light of their tablets.

It was midnight when they reached the bureau. Most floors of the main building were dark; only criminal investigation, the forensic laboratory and cybercrime remained brightly lit. Ceiling lights reflected from corridor tiles as footsteps echoed along empty passages.

Shen Yu’an went directly to the forensic laboratory, put on full protective equipment and entered the autopsy room. The metal table was cold, the body container brought into place, instruments making faint metallic sounds. Outside, Lu Zheng watched the working figure through glass. He did not interrupt. Leaning against the wall, he reviewed footage copied at the scene.
Frame after frame passed: empty park paths, moving shrubs. No trace of the suspect.

Interview records arrived on the tablet. Repeated comparisons of cleaners’, guards’ and property staff’s statements yielded only one firm lead: the black-clad figure a guard had seen before dawn three days earlier. Everything else was an unhelpful fragment.

Keyboards sounded continuously in the detachment office. The cybercrime team sifted enormous network logs for dark-web access. IP addresses filled the screens, most merely relay points, the true source hidden beneath layers of proxies.
A young officer brought printed interviews and placed them beside Lu Zheng.
“Everyone employed at the park has been checked. No one has a background in medical dissection. No outsider has applied for a short-term position in the past six months.”
Lu Zheng turned through the densely written pages.
“Widen it. Look at people who left dissection-related or surgical work in this city over the past year. Cross-check those who have lived abroad. Don’t limit it to current local residents.”
The officer recorded the instruction and left.

The autopsy room stayed lit. The examination took time. Shen Yu’an worked methodically, recording every cut and the condition of the bones, taking blood and tissue for testing. The ache in his left shoulder persisted. He adjusted his stance, shifting more weight to his right leg, without disturbing the rhythm of his hands.
Outside, black turned gradually to gray-blue. A faint morning light appeared. The city was not fully awake, and traffic remained sparse.

Beyond the glass, Lu Zheng was still in the corridor. A thick stack of paper files stood on the table; unfinished footage remained on the tablet. Now and then he looked toward the working figure, then returned to the files.
The laboratory door opened. Shen Yu’an emerged, outer protective layer removed, mask in his hand, a light sweat at his temple. He carried several pages of handwritten preliminary findings.

“Male, thirty-six to thirty-eight. The fatal injury is inside the chest: a sharp implement penetrated the organs. The external dismemberment was postmortem. Every cut follows professional anatomical entry angles. Stomach contents place death around two in the morning three days ago. Samples are in the laboratory. Drug and toxicology reports are pending.”
He handed over the pages. Lu Zheng took them and read each conclusion.
“The petals and stone-crevice samples?”
“Evidence processing has them. They’re comparing trace material and trying to establish where the flowers were bought.”
Lu Zheng closed the report and looked at his face. The overnight work had left a faint weariness in his eyes.
“There’s a bed in the room next door. Lie down for a while. I’ll have someone tell you when the results arrive.”
Shen Yu’an accepted without argument. Taking a paper cup of water from Lu Zheng, he went to the rest room at the end of the corridor. The door closed on the office noise.

The detachment continued at full pace. Dozens of monitors played footage while officers repeatedly reviewed junctions around the park. Vast files filled the servers. A four-day search began, drawing extensive personnel and resources into the hunt. Every line of inquiry pointed outward, toward the mysterious organization beyond their own circle.

At six-thirty, daylight spread over An’an’s buildings. Low mist softened the night’s chill. Early traffic began to move, faint sounds passing through the double glazing and breaking the office’s frozen silence.
The whole floor remained under bright artificial light. Rows of blue monitors filled the walls. Dozens of officers watched and typed, fully absorbed in the mass of footage. The tension did not ease.
The four-day comprehensive search was now fully underway.

At his desk, Lu Zheng repeatedly dragged the playback bar through the one-to-four-a.m. window around the sculpture park. Victim records, scene plans and interviews covered the desk in layers, their edges curling from repeated handling.
The victim had been identified.

Zhao Qiang, thirty-eight, unemployed, an An’an resident with three prior records for petty theft and group disturbances. He moved between rented rooms on the outskirts, with no settled home or social circle, distant relatives and irregular, varied contacts.
The associated records were unusually empty.

No background in surgery, anatomy or healthcare; no study of floral arrangement; no artistic work or recorded interest. His devices had never visited an overseas dark-web entrance. Nothing about him matched the expertise, aesthetics or evasion required for the ritual crimes.
He was simply a selected sacrifice. No personal dispute, no private grudge. A suitable vessel chosen to complete the organization’s ritual.
Lu Zheng stared at the empty park path on the screen, his brow hard.
Random sacrifice. Ordered ritual. No personal grievance. An exceptionally careful plan.
The killer’s objective was never a particular person. It was an ongoing, regular and reproducible performance of crime.
He opened the team’s work group and typed new orders, precise and without wasted words.

“Expand the search radius to eight kilometers. Prioritize solitary night walkers over the past week, people without recorded journeys and strangers repeatedly seen on unmonitored roads outside the city. Technical team: compare every abandoned blind spot around both scenes and compile overlaps. Interview team: revisit all park staff and verify unusual nighttime details individually.”
The message went out. Each group received it and resumed work without a break in coordination.
At the corridor’s end, the rest-room door was firmly closed.
The blackout curtains shut out daylight and sound, leaving the space dim and still.
Shen Yu’an lay flat on the folding bed, limbs relaxed, eyes lightly closed.
Everything about him suggested complete rest, exactly the sleep of someone exhausted after working all night.
But he was awake.

Alone and unobserved, the fractures in perception brought by schizophrenia slipped free of concealment. Distorted auditory hallucinations layered themselves deep in his hearing: scattered whispers, faint rubbing sounds, indistinct ritual murmurs. The sensory confusion others could not bear was a familiar part of his solitude.
The cold trough of bipolar depression covered him completely.
His body felt chilled and numb, emotion stripped away. There was neither fatigue nor relief after work. Only a dead, indifferent stillness.
He remembered the entire examination, every conversation and movement.

Lu Zheng turning to block the draft. The deliberately generous report deadline. The eyes on his injured shoulder. The constant watch. Shen Yu’an smiled faintly. “How touching, Officer Lu.” His fingertips tapped the bed frame twice, evenly, as if counting.
The noise slowly receded, leaving an echo circling in his ears. It did not hurt. It was simply loud. He opened his eyes, pupils adjusting to the darkness before settling.
The white water stains on the ceiling stayed in the same places. He had counted them. Seven.

He sat up smoothly, without the sluggishness of someone waking from exhausted sleep. Taking his uniform jacket from the chair, he dressed, fastened the last button and smoothed the collar. The mirror showed an expressionless face, clear eyes revealing nothing.
When he opened the door, the corridor lights made him narrow his eyes.

The office was busy. Someone hurried past with printed papers; someone checked camera time codes over the phone. The whiteboard was crowded with composite sketches, junction maps and the victim’s social network, red lines linking the clues.
Lu Zheng stood before it with a black marker, drawing a dotted line between the two scenes. His sleeves were rolled to his forearms, a little ink on his knuckles.
At the footsteps, he turned.
“Awake?”
Shen Yu’an approached, looking over the route map. His voice carried exactly the right trace of post-sleep roughness. “What time is it?”
“Nine-forty.” Lu Zheng capped the marker and picked up a plastic bag from the desk. “Soy milk and buns from the canteen. Still warm.”
Warmth came through the thin plastic. Shen Yu’an took it, his fingertips brushing Lu Zheng’s knuckles for less than half a second, naturally enough to seem accidental.
“Thank you, Team Leader Lu.”
He sat nearby and opened the straw, neither hurried nor slow. Lu Zheng turned back to the board and pointed at the line between the scenes.

“The technical results just came in. The two disposal sites sit at the east and west ends of the ring road, seventeen kilometers apart in a straight line. The locations weren’t random. Someone surveyed them along one route.”
Shen Yu’an bit into a bun, chewing steadily while following the finger.
“What about the overlapping blind spots?”

“Found one.” Lu Zheng circled an irregular patch. “The old machine-tool factory in the west. Abandoned for six years, two collapsed sections of wall, no private camera within three hundred meters. The public-security network doesn’t reach it either.”
He paused and lowered his voice. “If one person committed both crimes, it’s probably a transfer point.”
Shen Yu’an set down the soy milk and lightly rubbed the cup.
The old machine-tool factory.

Of course he knew it. At 4:17 a.m. three days earlier, he had shaken the last rose petal from his coat pocket onto a machine’s iron bed as the eastern sky began to gray. After clearing every trace, he climbed through the northern wall gap, entered a lane used by the morning market and walked two blocks among the first traders before hailing a night-shift taxi.
He had never raised his head.
“Should we go now?” His tone was a forensic physician’s ordinary question: calm, professional, without extra feeling.
Lu Zheng shook his head. “Field officers are already there, sealing it. They’re waiting for you to examine it.”
For you, not for the team.
Two passing officers heard it and neither slowed nor changed expression. Such words from Lu Zheng were as ordinary now as “stay safe.”
Shen Yu’an stood, put the remaining half-bun in its paper bag, crumpled it and threw it away.
“Let’s go.”
The factory was more ruined than expected.

Dead creeper covered the outer wall, branches like cracked veins on concrete. The iron front gate had been forced, its latch crooked beside a rusty chain. Three buildings formed a U. Long sections of roof had collapsed, letting slanting sunlight scatter over the floor.
Rust, damp soil and decaying plants filled the air.
Field officers had set a cordon. Two uniformed guards lifted the tape as Lu Zheng approached.
“Team Leader, the building on the east side has petal fragments and drag marks. Nothing unusual elsewhere yet.”
Lu Zheng nodded and stepped aside. “Dr. Shen first.”
Shen Yu’an crouched and put on gloves from his kit. As his fingers touched the ground, his gaze began a systematic sweep: threshold to corner, machine base to drainage channel.
The field team had bagged the petal fragments separately. He held the bag up to the light.
The same variety as at the sculpture park: white Carola roses, petal edges trimmed into clean cuts.

He returned the bag to the recorder. “Drag marks run from the center to the eastern wall. Pale scuffing, probably fabric or plastic sheeting. Petals are concentrated within half a meter on either side, consistent with dropping during transport.”
He rose and walked around the building.
Half a footprint lay in one corner, mostly covered with dust. He crouched again, placed a scale beside it and asked for a photograph. Size forty-one, athletic-shoe tread, the outer heel more worn.
“Compared with the impression outside the sculpture park?” he asked.
A technician checked the tablet. “Different tread. That was a size forty-three work boot.”
Shen Yu’an murmured assent and said no more.
Naturally the treads differed. He had deliberately worn another pair here. Changing shoes during transport was one of the ritual’s basic measures against investigation.
Lu Zheng stood at the entrance, arms folded, eyes following him.
As Shen Yu’an straightened, his left shoulder shifted slightly, like ordinary stiffness after crouching. He raised a hand to his neck and shoulder and rubbed twice.
Lu Zheng spoke from behind him.
“Down there too long?”
“I’m fine.” Shen Yu’an turned, expression neutral.
Lu Zheng came closer, glanced at the shoulder and turned to the technical team. “Perimeter finished?”

“Yes. Half a fingerprint at the wall gap, already recovered. A disposable food container with leftovers and half a bottle of water in the rubbish behind the factory. We don’t know whether they’re the suspect’s.”
“Send them for testing.”
It was past noon when they left.
The sun was fierce, the asphalt softened by heat, exhaust drifting in warm waves. Field officers stayed to continue searching while Lu Zheng drove Shen Yu’an back.
Air conditioning chilled their arms.
Shen Yu’an leaned in the passenger seat, watching the streets fall away. Tree shadows crossed his face frame by frame.
Lu Zheng held the wheel with one hand, the other elbow near the window. After a silence, he spoke.
“What time did you finish the autopsy?”
“After three.”
“Why didn’t you call me?”
Shen Yu’an turned slightly. “You didn’t need to stay up too.”
The answer was light, with just enough formality to preserve distance without seeming cold. A subordinate’s consideration for a superior, perfectly measured.
Lu Zheng swallowed and said nothing.

The car radio came alive with a technician’s voice. “Team Leader, the petal comparison is back. The white roses in both cases came from the same cut-flower wholesale market in the south. Same variety and batch.”
“Cameras at the market?”
“Yes, but old and very low resolution. No clear faces. We’re checking dispatch records from a week ago for large white-rose purchases.”
“Keep going.”
The radio went quiet.
Shen Yu’an looked back outside. His fingers tapped his knee twice, in exactly the rhythm he had used on the bed frame that morning.
The southern wholesale market.

He knew it. He had arrived at five in the morning, as it opened and wholesalers were still unloading. Mask and baseball cap on, he paid cash for two bunches of white roses and carried them in a black plastic bag. Less than four minutes, hardly a word exchanged.
Even recovered footage would show only a blurred masked figure.
The car entered the bureau compound and stopped. Lu Zheng removed the key and turned toward him.
“Nothing more for you this afternoon. Get some sleep in the office. I’ll have the lab reports put on your desk.”
Shen Yu’an paused briefly while releasing his seat belt, then nodded. “All right.”
He opened the door. As his foot touched the ground, Lu Zheng called him back.
“Shen Yu’an.”
He turned.
Lu Zheng sat with a hand still on the wheel. Light behind him left his features in shadow.
“Remember to change the shoulder dressing.”
Standing outside, Shen Yu’an curled his fingers almost imperceptibly.
“I will.”
He walked toward the building, back straight and pace steady.
Lu Zheng watched until he vanished behind the glass doors, then restarted the car and drove into the underground garage.

In the office, footage review continued. More red lines crossed the whiteboard. The flower source, the factory transfer point and the western surveillance blind spot were circled into a rough triangle.
Everyone was moving toward it.
No one imagined that its center was sitting in a chair in the third-floor forensic office, staring outside for two seconds before opening a drawer, taking a fresh autopsy form and beginning to write.
The pen moved neatly, with even pressure.
He wrote with complete attention, as though making something that had to be perfect.

alt.en: Lu Zheng shelters Shen Yu’an from the wind while technicians collect white rose petals at the sculpture park.
alt.zh: 雕塑公园里，陆峥替沈予安挡风，技术员采集白玫瑰花瓣。

zh: 笔锋在纸面上停了两秒，沈予安落下最后一个句号，把笔搁回笔帽里。
窗外的日头已经偏西，光线斜斜切过办公室的百叶窗，在桌面上切出一道道明暗相间的条纹。隔壁解剖室的冷柜压缩机嗡嗡作响，走廊尽头传来打印机吐纸的沙沙声。
他把尸检记录表装订好，起身走向陆峥的办公室。
门虚掩着，里面传来说话声。陆峥在打电话，语气压得很低，听不清具体内容，只偶尔蹦出"监控""走访""继续查"几个词。沈予安站在门口，屈指敲了两下门板。
里面的说话声停了。
沈予安推门进去，把装订好的报告放在陆峥桌角。"赵强的完整尸检记录，补了几处细节。胃内容物里检出少量地西泮残留，剂量不高，够让人失去反抗能力但不至于立刻昏迷。死亡时间锁在三天前凌晨一点到两点之间，和保安撞见黑影的时间基本对上。"
陆峥放下电话，拿过报告翻了两页。
"地西泮。"他重复了一遍这个词，指节在桌面上敲了敲，"处方药，管控类。"
"黑市也能弄到。"沈予安靠在桌沿，双手插在白大褂口袋里，"渠道太多，不好查。"
陆峥抬眼看他。下午的光从百叶窗缝里漏进来，在沈予安脸上切出一半明一半暗的轮廓。眼下有淡淡的青黑，是连续两晚没睡好的痕迹，演得恰到好处。
"你回去睡。"陆峥把报告合上，"晚上不用守着了，化验结果出来我让人送你家去。"
"也行。"沈予安没推辞，点头应下，转身往外走。
手刚搭上门把手，陆峥的声音又从后面追过来。
"肩膀怎么样。"
沈予安回头，脸上挂着一点恰到好处的疲惫笑意。"换药了，没事。"
陆峥盯着他看了两秒，没再说什么，挥了挥手让他走。
门带上的瞬间，沈予安脸上那点笑意一点一点褪干净，像拉上一层幕布。他沿着走廊往电梯口走，皮鞋踩在地砖上，声音清脆均匀。
地西泮。
他当然知道死者胃里有这个。三天前凌晨，他用注射器把稀释过的药液推进赵强颈动脉的时候，手表显示的时间是一点零七分。药量算得很准，够人瘫软四十分钟，够他完成所有步骤，不会中途醒过来挣扎。
赵强醒过一次。
在机床厂的水泥地上，那人的眼皮动了动，喉咙里发出含混的呜咽。沈予安蹲在旁边，手里握着解剖刀，安静等了三秒，确认对方只是意识模糊、还看不清人脸，才继续下刀。
整个过程没有任何情绪波动。像在处理一件流水线上的次品。
电梯到了，他走进去，按了负一层。
停车场空旷安静，灯管嗡嗡响着。他的车停在最里面的角落，一辆灰色的国产轿车，毫不起眼，和市局任何一个普通科员的代步车没区别。拉开车门坐进去，他没有立刻发动，而是靠在驾驶座椅背上，闭了一会儿眼。
幻听又来了。
这次不是细碎的低语，是一段模糊的旋律，像从很远的地方飘过来的圣歌，歌词听不清，音调反反复复盘旋在脑子里。他知道这是双相情感障碍转躁期的前兆，大脑开始自己制造声音，把现实和幻觉搅在一起。
他从扶手箱里摸出一个白色药瓶，倒出两片，干咽下去。
药片卡在喉咙里，有点苦。
发动车子，驶出停车场。傍晚高峰刚过，路面上的车还排着长队，刹车灯连成一片红色。他跟着车流慢慢往前挪，收音机里放着一档晚间新闻，主播用平稳的语调播报本市治安情况，语气里透着"一切正常"的官方口径。
沈予安听着，嘴角牵了一下。
一切正常。
他把车停在小区地下车库，上楼。房子是租的，两室一厅，装修简单，家具少得像样板间。玄关鞋柜上摆着一个相框，里面是他穿法医制服的证件照，笑得标准。
他踢掉皮鞋，赤脚走进客厅，把自己摔进沙发里。
天花板上的水渍形状和市局休息室那间不一样，他数了数，五块。
手机在口袋里震了一下。
他摸出来看，屏幕上是一条陌生号码发来的短信，内容只有六个字：
"玫瑰已签收。"
沈予安盯着那六个字看了三秒，指尖在屏幕上慢慢敲了两个字回去。
"下一株。"
发送。
他把手机扔到沙发另一端，仰面躺着，盯着天花板。
下一株。
组织的指令永远简洁，不需要多余的解释。上一场仪式完成得很漂亮，花瓣、解剖、藏尸点，全部按标准流程走，没有任何纰漏。警方的调查方向被牢牢锁在外部，监控盲区、随机受害者、专业手法，所有线索都指向一个不存在的"外部专业犯罪组织"。
没有人会怀疑到市局法医头上。
尤其是陆峥。
想到这个名字，沈予安的脑子里浮现出傍晚对方隔着百叶窗看他的眼神。那种眼神里有担心，有破例，有不加掩饰的特殊对待，像在看一件需要小心翼翼捧着的易碎品。
真可笑。
他闭上眼，躁期带来的亢奋感从脊椎底端慢慢爬上来，手指尖开始发麻，大脑转速越来越快，无数念头像走马灯一样转。他在脑子里复盘这两周的每一个细节：买花的路线、换鞋的时间、清理痕迹的顺序、和陆峥说过的每一句话、每一次眼神接触的分寸。
全部完美。
陆峥现在对他的信任度，大概到了九成。剩下那一成，是刑侦队长的本能警惕，不针对任何人，是职业惯性。用不了多久，那一成也会被他一点点磨掉。
他需要陆峥完全信任他。
因为下一场仪式，需要一个更贴近核心的位置。
手机又震了一下。
这次不是短信，是陆峥发来的微信。
"到家了？"
沈予安拿起来看了一眼，指尖在屏幕上敲了两个字。
"刚到。"
发完，他把手机扣在沙发上，起身去浴室洗澡。
热水从头顶浇下来，顺着锁骨往下淌。他站在花洒下面，闭着眼，水流声把幻听的旋律盖过去了一些。镜子上起了一层雾，他伸手抹了一把，看见里面的自己。
脸色苍白，眼窝有点深，嘴唇没什么血色。
这张脸长得太干净了，干净到任何人看了都不会往连环杀手那边想。他一直知道这是自己最大的伪装武器。陆峥第一次见他的时候，大概也是这么觉得的——一个安安静静、业务过硬、需要被照顾的年轻法医。
真是浪费了这张脸。
他关了水，扯下毛巾围在腰上，走出浴室。
手机屏幕又亮了。
陆峥："早点睡，明天上午碰头会。"
沈予安看了一眼，没回。
他把手机扔到床头柜上，躺下来，拉过被子盖住半边身子。窗帘没拉严，一道城市的夜光从缝隙里漏进来，在天花板上投下一道细长的光带。
幻听的旋律还在转，越来越响，像有人在他脑子里敲钟。
他翻了个身，把脸埋进枕头里。
第二天上午九点，支队会议室。
长桌周围坐满了人，白板上贴着两起命案的现场照片、死者身份信息、监控点位分布图。空气里飘着速溶咖啡的苦味和打印机墨粉的味道。
陆峥站在白板前，手里捏着一支马克笔。
"过去四十八小时，各部门汇报进展。技术组先说。"
技术组长推了推眼镜，翻开手里的平板。"花瓣来源追查到城南批发市场，监控覆盖不到摊位内部，商贩记不清具体买家，但根据出货记录，案发前两天有一笔二十扎白玫瑰的批量订单，现金结算，自提。订单登记的姓名是假的，电话也是空号。"
"鞋印比对呢。"
"机床厂提取到的四十一码运动鞋印，和全国前科数据库比对过，没有匹配。雕塑公园外围的四十三码工装靴印，也没有结果。"
"指纹。"
"围墙缺口那半枚指纹，正在比对。量太少，可识别点不多，出结果可能还要等。"
陆峥点头，转向走访组。
走访组的女警翻了翻笔记本。"死者赵强的社会关系全部捋了一遍。这人混得很差，朋友少，债主多。我们找了三个和他有过来往的人，全部有案发时段的不在场证明。最近和他起过冲突的是一个开棋牌室的老板，因为欠账被赵强砸过一台麻将机。但那老板有棋牌室监控，案发当天晚上从十点到凌晨五点，他一直在店里打牌，二十多个人能作证。"
"仇杀方向排除？"
"基本排除。赵强这种人，被杀大概率不是因为仇，更像随机被挑中。"
会议室里安静了几秒。
陆峥在白板上"随机受害者"四个字下面画了一道横线。
"网安那边呢。"
网安组的年轻人接话，声音带着熬夜后的沙哑。"暗网La Rose Éternelle的新访问记录又冒出来了，IP跳转了七层，最终出口在境外。和上一起案子比对，用的是同一套加密链路。我们顺着子域名往下挖，发现这个站点最近新增了一个英文板块，内容都是关于'仪式美学'的论文和图片，访问量很小，注册用户不到五十个。"
"能定位到注册者吗。"
"难。全部走洋葱路由，真实身份藏得很深。但我们锁定了一个活跃ID，最近三个月在板块里发了七条帖子，内容都是关于凶案现场构图的分析，用词很专业，像内部人士。"
"持续盯。"
"明白。"
汇报一圈下来，所有线索都像拳头打在棉花上。花瓣来源断了，鞋印指纹没匹配上，死者社会关系干净得反常，暗网线索藏在境外摸不到实体。
会议室里的气氛沉下来。
陆峥把马克笔往桌上一放，目光扫过全场。
"换个思路。"他在白板上两起案发现场的位置之间画了一条线，"凶手选点不是随机的。雕塑公园在城东，机床厂在城西，两个点连起来，刚好穿过市中心。中间这条线，你们给我一寸一寸查。"
他在这条线的中点位置点了一下。
"凶手踩点不可能只踩两个点。他一定走过更多地方，看过更多监控死角，选过更多备选位置。我们找不到他，是因为我们只盯着案发地查。把范围拉宽，沿着这条线，把所有符合'监控盲区、人流量低、隐蔽性强'特征的地点全部列出来，一个一个过。"
队员们低头记笔记，键盘敲击声此起彼伏。
沈予安坐在长桌最靠边的位置，手里转着一支笔，听得很认真。
他知道陆峥说的这条线。
那条线确实穿过市中心，而且经过三个他实地踩过、最后放弃的备选点。一个是旧图书馆地下室，一个是废弃游泳馆，还有一个是城南高架桥下的涵洞。这三个地方的隐蔽性都够，但要么通风太差，要么人流量比预估的大，要么结构不符合花瓣摆放的对称要求。
他最后选了雕塑公园。
陆峥的刑侦嗅觉确实敏锐。顺着这条线查下去，迟早能摸到那三个被放弃的备选点。到时候现场就算清理得再干净，也总会留下一点什么。
不过没关系。
就算查到了备选点，也查不到他头上。那三个地方他都戴了手套鞋套，走的时候连一根头发都没留。
会议开了一个多小时。散会的时候，队员们陆续起身往外走，椅子腿蹭着地面发出刺耳的声响。
沈予安收笔记本的动作慢了半拍，等其他人走得差不多了，才起身。
陆峥还站在白板前，盯着那条线出神。
"陆队。"沈予安走到他旁边，"中午食堂有排骨，去晚了没了。"
陆峥回过头，看了他一眼，眼神里还带着思考的沉淀。"你先去，我把这几个点位标完就来。"
沈予安点头，转身往外走。
走到门口的时候，他像是忽然想起什么，停下来回头。
"对了，昨天化验室那边说，花瓣上检出了少量泥土残留，成分和机床厂地面的土壤样本比对上了。"
陆峥眉头动了一下。"什么时候的事。"
"今早刚出的结果，本来想开会的时候说，忘了。"沈予安语气自然，"泥土里有微量机油成分，机床厂那种地方多的是机器漏油，吻合度很高。基本可以确认，凶手是在机床厂完成分尸和花瓣布置，再转运到雕塑公园藏进去的。"
这个信息是真的。
他确实在机床厂处理过尸体，花瓣也是在那里摆好造型才装车运走的。泥土残留只是时间问题，化验室早晚能查出来。他主动说出来，反而显得他专业、上心、时刻跟进每一条物证线索。
陆峥听完，点了点头。"这个线索重要。我让技术组顺着机床厂周边再扩一圈监控。"
"好。"沈予安应了一声，推门出去了。
走廊里阳光充足，透过落地窗洒在地砖上。他往食堂方向走，脚步平稳，脑子里在盘算下一件事。
陆峥的思路转得很快。按照这个速度，四天之内摸到机床厂周边的监控死角是大概率事件。他需要在那之前，把下一场仪式的备选位置提前想好，留好下一步的棋。
组织那边催得紧。"下一株"三个字不是随便说说的，下一次出手的时间窗口，大概就在十天之内。
他推开食堂的门，喧闹声扑面而来。打饭窗口排着长队，菜香混着人声。他端了餐盘找了个角落坐下，拿起筷子，一口一口慢慢吃。
排骨炖得有点老，他嚼得很认真。
脑子里已经在画图了——下一个场地的结构、花瓣的数量、分尸的角度、藏尸点的选择。
这场游戏才刚开始。
第三天下午三点，外勤组在旧图书馆地下室找到了痕迹。
陆峥赶到的时候，地下室入口的铁门已经被掀开，两个外勤队员打着手电筒蹲在地上，光柱在潮湿的水泥地面上来回扫。空气里混着霉味和尘土味，脚下的积水没过鞋底，凉得刺骨。
"陆队。"蹲在前面的队员回头，手电光往上抬了抬，"您看这儿。"
陆峥蹲下去，指尖拨开地上一层薄灰。
灰尘上面有几道浅浅的压痕，形状不规则，像是放过什么重物之后挪开留下的。压痕边缘还沾着一点暗红色的污渍，已经干硬发黑。
"取样。"陆峥站起身，目光扫过整个地下室空间。
废弃图书馆的地下室大概两百平米，水泥墙皮大面积脱落，露出里面发黑的砖体。头顶管道纵横，有几根还在往下滴水，滴答声在空旷的地下室里来回撞。墙角堆着破书架和烂纸箱，地上散落着发霉的旧书，纸页黏成一团，一碰就碎。
手电光扫到西墙根的时候，陆峥停住了。
"那边。"
队员把光打过去。
墙根处的灰尘上，有一道细长的划痕，约莫二十公分长，边缘整齐，像被什么锋利的金属片划出来的。划痕旁边还有几个不完整的鞋印，被积水泡得模糊，只能看出个大概轮廓。
"和机床厂的鞋印比对过吗。"
"技术员正在采，得回去才能出结果。"
陆峥绕着地下室走了一圈。出口有两个，一个是他进来的正门，另一个在北墙，是一扇锈死的消防铁门，门上挂着粗重的铁链，铁链锁已经被剪断了，断口崭新。
他蹲下去摸了摸断口。铁屑还带着金属的凉意，断口平整，剪切工具很锋利。
"这里被人用过。"陆峥站直身体，"时间不长。"
技术组长从门口钻进来，裤腿上沾了泥点。他听完汇报，蹲在那道划痕旁边看了半天，眉头拧起来。
"陆队，您觉不觉得这划痕的走向，和雕塑公园那道……"
他没说完，但陆峥听懂了。
雕塑公园的花岗岩夹层内壁上，也有一道类似的细长划痕，当时大家以为是石材加工留下的。现在对照起来，两道划痕的角度、长度、深度，几乎一模一样。
"凶手在这里试过刀。"陆峥的声音在地下室里撞出回音。
他掏出手机拨了个号，电话响了三声被接起来。
"沈予安，你过来一趟。旧图书馆地下室，地址我发你。带勘验箱。"
挂了电话，陆峥把手机揣回兜里，转头对技术组长说："把整个地下室的地面全部扫一遍，每一寸都拍高清照。另外调一下这栋楼周边的监控，看看最近有没有人从消防通道进出。"
四十分钟后，沈予安到了。
他从车上下来的时候，手里拎着勘验箱，白大褂外面套了一件深色冲锋衣。下午的太阳还毒，他额角出了一层薄汗，发丝贴在鬓角。
"什么情况。"他走到陆峥面前，声音平稳。
陆峥把现场情况简要讲了一遍。沈予安听完，点了下头，戴上手套，蹲到那道划痕旁边。
他从箱子里取出比例尺，贴在划痕边缘，让记录员拍照。又用棉签取了一点墙根处的暗红色污渍样本，装进证物管里，拧紧盖子。
"划痕深度两毫米左右，宽度均匀，锋利刃具造成。"沈予安的声音不高，刚好让旁边的人听清，"和雕塑公园花岗岩夹层内壁那道划痕，工具特征吻合。"
他站起身，绕着地下室走了半圈，在那几个模糊鞋印旁边蹲下，用手电侧着光照了照。
"鞋印纹路看不完整，但后跟磨损方向和机床厂那枚四十一码的鞋印接近。"
技术组长在旁边飞快记笔记。
沈予安蹲在地上，视线扫过地面的每一寸灰尘。他的动作很慢，很稳，像在欣赏一幅画。
他当然知道这道划痕是怎么来的。
两周前他在这里试过刀。选的是和作案同款的解剖刀片，在水泥墙上划了七次，前六次角度不对，第七次才找到最顺手的发力角度。那堆暗红色污渍，是他用一只野猫做试切实验留下的。猫是从后巷捡的，流浪猫，瘦得只剩一把骨头，掐死之后拖进地下室，下刀的位置和角度全部模拟正式流程。
整个过程持续了四十分钟。清理现场花了一个半小时。
他站起身，拍了拍膝盖上的灰。
"初步判断，这里是凶手的预演点。"沈予安转向陆峥，语气是标准的工作汇报口吻，"他在这里练习过下刀角度和搬运路径，确认没问题之后才去了雕塑公园。"
陆峥看着他，目光沉了沉。
"也就是说，他踩的点不止这两个。"
"对。"沈予安点头，"一个做事这么周密的人，不会只试一次。我们找到的这两个，可能只是他备选清单上的两个。"
地下室里安静了几秒，只有水滴声在响。
陆峥的下巴绷紧了。他原本以为沿着两个案发点连线查，最多找到一两个备选位置。现在看来，凶手的谨慎程度远超预估——这是一个会反复演练、反复测试、反复推翻重来的人。
"扩大搜索范围。"陆峥对身后的队员说，"沿着这条线，把所有符合条件的废弃建筑全部列出来。地下室、旧厂房、空置仓库，一个都别漏。"
队员应了一声，转身出去安排。
沈予安把勘验箱扣好，拎在手里。地下室光线昏暗，他的脸半明半暗，表情看不出什么。
"泥土样本要不要再取一组。"他问。
"取。"陆峥说，"和机床厂、雕塑公园的土壤做交叉比对。如果三个地方都有共同成分，说明他用了同一种运输工具或者铺垫材料。"
沈予安蹲回去取样的时候，陆峥站在旁边看了他一会儿。
地下室的潮气压得人胸口发闷，沈予安蹲在地上，后背的衣服被汗洇湿了一小块，贴在肩胛骨上。他取样的动作很稳，手腕不抖，呼吸节奏也没变。
陆峥忽然开口："上去透透气吧，里面闷。"
沈予安手上的动作停了半秒，随即继续把棉签塞进证物管。
"快好了。"
"先上去。"陆峥的语气不容商量，"剩下的让技术员来。"
沈予安这才直起身，摘了手套，跟着陆峥往外走。
出了地下室，外面的阳光晃得人眯眼。旧图书馆门口是一条梧桐树掩映的老街，路面坑坑洼洼，两边停满了车。陆峥从车里拿了一瓶矿泉水递过去，沈予安接过来，拧开喝了一口。
"肩膀怎么样。"陆峥靠在车门上，看着他。
"还行。"沈予安把瓶盖拧回去，"地下室蹲久了有点酸，上来就好了。"
陆峥的目光在他左肩停了一秒，没再说什么。
两人站在树荫底下，看着外勤队员进进出出。老街上很安静，远处传来收废品的喇叭声，循环播放着干巴巴的调子。
"你觉得他下一步会在哪动手。"陆峥忽然问。
沈予安偏过头看他。
这个问题他不需要想。下一场仪式的位置他已经定好了，就在城南的老自来水厂，一个他踩过五次点、确认过所有监控盲区的地方。时间窗口在八天之后，那天晚上月全食，整座城市的夜间亮度会比平时低三成。
但他脸上的表情恰到好处地迟疑了一下，像在认真思考。
"说不好。"沈予安把矿泉水瓶在手里转了半圈，"他选点的标准很一致——隐蔽、监控盲区、结构适合藏尸。安市符合这些条件的地方，两只手数得过来。顺着这个方向筛，应该能缩小范围。"
陆峥点了点头，目光望向街尽头。
"我让人把全市的废弃建筑全部过一遍。"
沈予安没接话，靠在车门上，视线落在路面的裂缝上。
裂缝里长出一根杂草，被太阳晒得发蔫。
他脑子里在算另一笔账。陆峥的速度比他预估的快了半天。旧图书馆这个点本来是他准备放弃之后再也不碰的，没想到还是被翻出来了。好在地下室清理得足够干净，那只猫的尸体早就处理掉了，现场能留下的只有划痕和鞋印——这些就算比对上，也只能证明"有人来过"，证明不了"是谁来过"。
风险可控。
真正需要小心的，是接下来的八天。
傍晚六点，陆峥办公室。
白板上又多了两个红圈——旧图书馆地下室和废弃游泳馆。两个点和雕塑公园、机床厂连在一起，刚好围成一个不规则的菱形。菱形的中心位置，是一片正在拆迁的老居民区。
陆峥站在白板前，手里捏着马克笔，指尖在那片拆迁区的位置敲了敲。
"这里。"他转过身，看向围在桌边的几个核心队员，"凶手踩过的点全部集中在这个菱形范围里。他的活动半径不会超出这个圈。"
技术组长凑过来看了一眼。"陆队，您是说他住在这附近？"
"不一定是住。"陆峥在拆迁区的位置画了个叉，"至少他熟悉这片区域的每一条巷子、每一个监控探头。一个外地人做不到这个程度。"
会议室里安静了几秒。
走访组的女警翻了翻笔记本。"这片老城区住的都是老人，年轻人早搬空了。拆迁公告贴了半年，一直没动工。白天还好，晚上黑灯瞎火的，连个路灯都没有。"
"那就从这片开始扫。"陆峥把马克笔往桌上一放，"挨家挨户敲门，查最近三个月有没有外来租户、有没有人半夜进出、有没有人在附近徘徊过。重点查独居、无业、有医学背景的男性。"
队员们记下指令，陆续起身往外走。
沈予安坐在角落的椅子上，手里转着一支笔，从头到尾没说话。
等人走得差不多了，他才站起身，把勘验箱拎起来。
"我先回检验科，把今天取的样本送过去。"
"嗯。"陆峥低头整理桌上的文件，头也没抬，"晚上别加班了，早点回去。"
沈予安应了一声，推门出去。
走廊里空无一人，白炽灯管嗡嗡响着。他走到电梯口，按了下行键，等电梯的时候掏出手机看了一眼。
屏幕上没有新消息。
他把手机揣回兜里，电梯门开了，走进去按了负一层。
车开出市局大门的时候，晚高峰刚过，路面上的车比白天少了一些。他沿着熟悉的路线开，经过一个十字路口的时候，红灯亮了，他停下来等。
旁边车道停着一辆黑色轿车，车窗半开。
沈予安的目光随意扫过去，和驾驶座上的人对上了眼。
那人三十来岁，寸头，下巴上有一道浅疤，穿着一件深灰色短袖。他看了沈予安一眼，表情没什么变化，像看一个普通路人。
绿灯亮了。
黑色轿车先动，汇入车流往前开。沈予安跟在后面，保持着正常的车距。
三个路口之后，黑色轿车拐进了一条小巷。沈予安没有跟进去，继续沿着主干道往前开，在前面一个红绿灯口掉头，从另一条路回了小区。
他把车停进车库，坐在驾驶座上没动，手指在方向盘上敲了两下。
寸头，下巴有疤。
他认得这个人。代号"修剪匠"，组织里负责收尾和清理的执行者。比他高两个层级，平时不直接参与仪式，只在需要善后的时候出手。
修剪匠出现在安市，说明上层开始关注这盘棋的进度了。
沈予安推开车门，下车，锁车，走进电梯。
电梯镜子里映出他的脸，还是那副没什么表情的样子。
修剪匠的出现不是好事。上层派自己人过来盯着，意味着他们对这场游戏的期待值很高，高到需要派人到场确认。
他需要把戏演得更真一点。
回到家，他把勘验箱扔在玄关，走进厨房倒了一杯水。水杯举到嘴边的时候，他停住了。
幻听又来了。
这次是一个男人的声音，很低，贴着耳朵说："别露破绽。"
沈予安面无表情地把水喝下去，把杯子放进水槽。
他走到窗边，撩开窗帘一角往下看。
小区门口的路灯底下，停着一辆黑色轿车。车窗贴了深色膜，看不清里面有没有人。
修剪匠。
他放下窗帘，转身走向浴室。
热水打开，蒸汽弥漫上来。他站在花洒下面，闭着眼，水流砸在头顶，把幻听的声音盖过去大半。
这场游戏才到中盘他还有足够的牌可以打。
en: The pen paused over the paper for two seconds. Shen Yu’an added the final period and fitted the pen back into its cap.

Outside, the sun had already moved west. Light slanted through the office blinds, cutting alternating strips of brightness and shadow across the desk. The mortuary refrigerator hummed in the adjoining autopsy room. At the end of the corridor, a printer rustled as it fed out paper.
He stapled the autopsy records together and went to Lu Zheng’s office.

The door stood ajar. Lu was on the phone, speaking too quietly for Shen to make out more than the occasional word: “surveillance,” “interviews,” “keep looking.” Shen stopped outside and knocked twice with his knuckles.
The voice inside fell silent.
“Come in.”

Shen pushed open the door and set the bound report on the corner of Lu’s desk. “Zhao Qiang’s complete autopsy report. I’ve added a few details. We detected traces of diazepam in the stomach contents. Not a high dose—enough to leave him unable to resist without making him lose consciousness immediately. Time of death is between one and two a.m. three days ago. That broadly matches the time the security guard saw the figure.”
Lu put down the phone, picked up the report, and turned a couple of pages.
“Diazepam.” He repeated the word, tapping the desk with his knuckles. “A controlled prescription drug.”
“You can get it on the black market, too.” Shen leaned against the edge of the desk, both hands in his lab-coat pockets. “Too many possible channels. It won’t be easy to trace.”

Lu looked up at him. Afternoon light filtered through the blinds, dividing Shen’s face between light and shadow. Faint darkness beneath his eyes suggested two nights of poor sleep. The performance was pitched exactly right.
“Go home and sleep.” Lu closed the report. “You don’t need to stay tonight. When the test results come in, I’ll have someone bring them to your place.”
“All right.” Shen made no objection. He nodded and turned to leave.
His hand had just reached the door handle when Lu’s voice followed him.
“How’s the shoulder?”
Shen looked back with a small, appropriately tired smile. “The dressing’s been changed. It’s fine.”
Lu watched him for two seconds, then said nothing more and waved him out.
The instant the door closed, the smile drained from Shen’s face, as though a curtain had fallen. He walked toward the elevators, his leather shoes striking the tiles in crisp, even beats.
Diazepam.

Of course he knew it was in the victim’s stomach. Three nights ago, when he had injected the diluted drug into Zhao Qiang’s carotid artery, his watch had read 1:07 a.m. He had calculated the amount precisely: enough to leave the man limp for forty minutes, enough to finish every step without him waking and struggling halfway through.
Zhao Qiang had woken once.

On the machine-tool factory’s concrete floor, the man’s eyelids had fluttered and an indistinct whimper had risen in his throat. Shen had crouched beside him, scalpel in hand, and waited quietly for three seconds. Only after confirming that Zhao was still dazed and unable to distinguish a face had he resumed cutting.
He had felt nothing throughout. It was like dealing with a defective item on an assembly line.
The elevator arrived. He stepped inside and pressed B1.

The parking garage was spacious and quiet, its fluorescent tubes humming. His car stood in the farthest corner: an unremarkable gray Chinese sedan, no different from the commuter car of any ordinary employee at the Municipal Public Security Bureau. He opened the door and got in, but did not start the engine immediately. Instead, he leaned back and closed his eyes for a while.
The auditory hallucinations had returned.

This time it was not a scatter of whispers but an indistinct melody, like a hymn drifting from very far away. He could not make out the words. The tune circled endlessly in his head. He recognized it as a warning of his bipolar disorder shifting toward mania: his brain beginning to manufacture sounds, stirring reality and hallucination together.
He took a white pill bottle from the center console, shook out two tablets, and swallowed them dry.
They caught in his throat, tasting faintly bitter.

He started the engine and drove out. The evening rush had just passed, but long lines of cars remained, their brake lights merging into a red field. He inched forward with the traffic. An evening news program played on the radio, the presenter reporting on public order in a steady voice that carried the official assurance that everything was normal.
Listening, Shen gave a slight twitch of his lips.
Everything was normal.

He parked in his apartment complex’s underground garage and went upstairs. The apartment was rented: two bedrooms and a living room, simply decorated, with so little furniture it resembled a show flat. A framed ID photograph stood on the shoe cabinet by the entrance. In it, he wore his forensic uniform and a perfectly standard smile.
He kicked off his shoes, walked barefoot into the living room, and dropped onto the sofa.
The water stains on the ceiling were different from those in the bureau’s rest room. He counted them. Five.
His phone vibrated in his pocket.
He took it out. A text from an unfamiliar number lit the screen. It contained only a short message:
“The rose has been received.”
Shen stared at the message for three seconds, then slowly tapped out his reply.
“The next rose.”
Send.
He tossed the phone to the other end of the sofa and lay on his back, staring at the ceiling.
The next rose.

The organization’s instructions were always concise. No further explanation was needed. The last ritual had been executed beautifully: the petals, the dissection, the concealment site, every part of the standard procedure without a single flaw. The police investigation was firmly directed outward. Surveillance blind spots, a randomly chosen victim, professional technique—every clue pointed to a nonexistent “external professional criminal organization.”
No one would suspect a forensic physician at the municipal bureau.
Least of all Lu Zheng.

At the thought of that name, Shen recalled the way Lu had looked at him through the slatted afternoon light. There had been worry in that gaze, exceptions made for him, undisguised special treatment—as though he were something fragile that had to be held with exquisite care.
How ridiculous.

He closed his eyes. The exhilaration of the manic phase crept upward from the base of his spine. His fingertips began to tingle. His mind spun faster and faster, thoughts wheeling like a revolving lantern. He reviewed every detail of the past two weeks: the route he had taken to buy flowers, when he had changed shoes, the order in which he had cleaned the traces, every sentence he had said to Lu, the precise measure of every exchange of looks.
All of it perfect.

Lu’s trust in him was probably at ninety percent now. The remaining ten percent was the instinctive caution of a criminal investigation team leader, directed at no one in particular, merely professional habit. Before long, Shen would wear that down as well.
He needed Lu to trust him completely.
Because the next ritual required a position closer to the center.
His phone vibrated again.
This time it was a WeChat message from Lu, not a text.
“Home yet?”
Shen picked it up, glanced at it, and tapped out a brief reply.
“Just got in.”
He sent it, placed the phone facedown on the sofa, and went to shower.

Hot water poured over his head and ran down his collarbones. He stood beneath the spray with his eyes closed. The sound of the water drowned out some of the phantom melody. Steam clouded the mirror. He wiped it with his hand and saw himself.
Pale skin, slightly hollow eyes, little color in his lips.

His face looked too innocent. So innocent that no one who saw it would think of a serial killer. He had always known it was his most effective disguise. When Lu first met him, he had probably seen exactly that—a quiet, capable young forensic physician who needed looking after.
What a waste of a face.
He turned off the water, wrapped a towel around his waist, and left the bathroom.
The phone screen lit up again.
Lu Zheng: “Get an early night. Briefing tomorrow morning.”
Shen glanced at it and did not answer.

He tossed the phone onto the bedside table, lay down, and drew the quilt over half his body. The curtains were not quite closed. A sliver of city light leaked through the gap, laying a long, narrow stripe across the ceiling.
The melody kept circling, growing louder, as though someone were ringing a bell inside his head.
He turned over and buried his face in the pillow.
Nine the next morning. The detachment’s conference room.

Every seat around the long table was occupied. Crime-scene photographs from both homicides, the victims’ details, and maps of surveillance coverage filled the whiteboard. The bitter smell of instant coffee mingled with printer toner.
Lu stood at the whiteboard with a marker in his hand.
“Progress over the past forty-eight hours. Technical team first.”

The technical team leader adjusted his glasses and opened his tablet. “We traced the petals to the wholesale market in the south of the city. The cameras don’t cover the interiors of the stalls, and the vendors can’t remember individual buyers. But the sales records show a bulk order of twenty bunches of white roses two days before the crime. Cash payment, collected in person. The name on the order was false, and the phone number is disconnected.”
“The shoe-print comparisons?”

“We checked the size forty-one trainer print from the machine-tool factory against the national criminal records database. No match. Nothing on the size forty-three work-boot print outside the sculpture park either.”
“Fingerprints?”
“We’re still comparing the partial print from the gap in the wall. There isn’t much of it, and there are few identifiable points. It may take longer.”
Lu nodded and turned to the canvassing team.

A female officer consulted her notebook. “We’ve gone through all of Zhao Qiang’s social connections. He wasn’t doing well—few friends, plenty of creditors. We located three people who had dealings with him. All have alibis for the relevant period. His most recent dispute was with a mahjong-parlor owner. Zhao smashed one of the man’s mahjong tables over a debt. But the owner’s security footage shows him playing cards in the shop from ten that night until five the next morning. More than twenty people can corroborate it.”
“So we can rule out a revenge killing?”
“More or less. With someone like Zhao Qiang, this probably wasn’t personal. It looks more as though he was picked at random.”
The room fell silent for a few seconds.
Lu underlined RANDOM VICTIM on the whiteboard.
“What about cybercrime?”

A young man from the cybercrime team spoke, his voice rough from lack of sleep. “New access records have surfaced for La Rose Éternelle on the dark web. The IP route passes through seven hops, with the final exit overseas. It uses the same encrypted connection as in the previous case. We followed the subdomains and found a recently added English-language section. It contains papers and images about ‘ritual aesthetics.’ Traffic is very low, with fewer than fifty registered users.”
“Can you identify the people who registered?”

“It’s difficult. They all use onion routing, and their real identities are buried deep. But we’ve isolated one active account. It posted seven times over the last three months, all analyses of crime-scene composition. The terminology is very professional. It reads like someone with inside knowledge.”
“Keep watching it.”
“Understood.”

By the end of the reports, every lead felt like a punch thrown into cotton. The flower trail had gone cold. Neither shoe prints nor fingerprints had produced a match. The victim’s social connections were unusually free of useful leads. The dark-web trail lay overseas, beyond anything they could physically reach.
The atmosphere in the room grew heavy.
Lu set the marker on the table and looked around.

“Let’s approach it differently.” He drew a line between the two crime-scene locations on the whiteboard. “The killer didn’t choose these places at random. The sculpture park is east of the city, the machine-tool factory west. Join the two, and the line runs straight through the city center. I want every inch of that line examined.”
He tapped its midpoint.

“The killer can’t have scouted only two places. He must have visited others, checked other surveillance blind spots, considered other alternatives. We haven’t found him because we’ve concentrated on the crime scenes. Widen the search. Along this line, list every location with poor camera coverage, little foot traffic, and good concealment. Check them one by one.”
The officers bent over their notes. Keyboards clattered around the table.
Shen sat at its farthest edge, turning a pen between his fingers and listening attentively.
He knew the line Lu was talking about.

It did pass through the city center, and through three locations he had personally scouted before rejecting them: the old library basement, an abandoned swimming pool, and a culvert beneath the southern overpass. All three offered enough concealment. But one had poor ventilation, another more passersby than expected, and another a structure unsuited to the symmetrical arrangement of petals.
In the end, he had chosen the sculpture park.

Lu’s investigative instincts were sharp. If they followed that line, sooner or later they would reach the three rejected sites. However thoroughly a place had been cleaned, there was always something left behind.
But that did not matter.
Even if they found those sites, they would not find him. He had worn gloves and shoe covers at all three. He had not left so much as a hair.
The meeting lasted more than an hour. When it ended, officers rose and filed out, chair legs scraping harshly across the floor.
Shen took a little longer than necessary to gather his notebook. Only when most of the others had left did he stand.
Lu remained at the whiteboard, staring at the line.
“Team Leader Lu.” Shen came up beside him. “The canteen has ribs for lunch. They’ll be gone if you’re late.”
Lu turned to look at him, his thoughts still lingering in his eyes. “You go ahead. I’ll finish marking these locations and join you.”
Shen nodded and headed for the door.
At the threshold, he stopped and turned as if something had just occurred to him.
“Oh, by the way. The lab said yesterday they found traces of soil on the petals. They match the samples from the machine-tool factory floor.”
Lu’s brow shifted. “When did that come through?”

“First thing this morning. I meant to mention it in the meeting and forgot.” Shen’s tone was natural. “There are traces of machine oil in the soil. A place like that factory has plenty of leaking machinery. It’s a close match. We can basically confirm that the killer dismembered the body and arranged the petals at the factory, then moved everything to the sculpture park for concealment.”
The information was true.

He had indeed dealt with the body at the factory. He had arranged the petals there before loading everything into the car. It was only a matter of time before the lab identified the soil. Volunteering the information made him appear professional, conscientious, and attentive to every piece of physical evidence.
Lu nodded when he had finished. “That’s important. I’ll have the technical team widen the camera search around the factory.”
“Good.” Shen pushed open the door and left.
Sunlight flooded the corridor through floor-to-ceiling windows and spilled across the tiles. He walked steadily toward the canteen, already calculating what came next.

Lu changed direction quickly. At this rate, there was a good chance he would locate the blind spots around the factory within four days. Before then, Shen needed to settle on alternatives for the next ritual and prepare his next move.
The organization was pressing him. “The next rose” was no idle phrase. The window for his next action would probably fall within ten days.

He opened the canteen door and walked into a wave of noise. Long queues stretched before the serving counters, food aromas mingling with conversation. He took a tray, found a corner, sat down, and began eating slowly with his chopsticks.
The ribs were a little overcooked. He chewed with great attention.
In his mind, he was already drawing plans—the layout of the next site, the number of petals, the angles of dismemberment, the place to conceal the body.
The game had only just begun.
At three in the afternoon on the third day, the field team found traces in the old library basement.

By the time Lu arrived, the iron door at the basement entrance had been forced open. Two officers crouched on the floor with flashlights, their beams sweeping the damp concrete. The air smelled of mold and dust. Standing water rose above the soles of his shoes, cold enough to bite.
“Team Leader Lu.” The officer in front looked back and lifted his flashlight. “Here.”
Lu crouched and brushed aside a thin layer of dust with his fingertips.
Several shallow, irregular impressions marked the dust, as if something heavy had rested there and then been moved. A little dark-red staining clung to their edges, dried hard and almost black.
“Take samples.” Lu stood and surveyed the basement.

The abandoned library’s basement covered roughly two hundred square meters. Large patches of plaster had fallen from the concrete walls, exposing blackened brick beneath. Pipes crisscrossed overhead; several still dripped, the sound echoing through the empty space. Broken bookshelves and rotting cardboard boxes were piled in the corners. Moldy books lay scattered across the floor, their pages stuck together in clumps that crumbled at a touch.
When the flashlight swept across the base of the west wall, Lu stopped.
“Over there.”
The officer directed the beam toward it.

A narrow scratch, about twenty centimeters long, ran through the dust at the wall’s base. Its edges were clean, as if a sharp piece of metal had made it. Beside it were several incomplete shoe prints, blurred by standing water until only their general outlines remained.
“Have you compared them with the prints from the factory?”
“The technicians are lifting them now. We’ll need to take them back before we have results.”

Lu walked around the basement. There were two exits: the main entrance he had used and a rusted iron fire door in the north wall. A heavy chain hung from it. The chain lock had been cut, the cut surfaces fresh.
He crouched and touched one. The metal filings were still cold; the cut was smooth, made with a sharp tool.
“Someone’s been using this place.” Lu straightened. “Recently.”
The technical team leader ducked through the doorway, mud spattering his trouser legs. After hearing the report, he crouched by the scratch and studied it, his brow tightening.
“Team Leader Lu, doesn’t the direction of this scratch remind you of the one at the sculpture park…?”
He did not finish, but Lu understood.

There had been a similarly narrow scratch on the inner wall of the granite cavity at the sculpture park. At the time, everyone had assumed it was left when the stone was worked. Compared now, the two scratches were almost identical in angle, length, and depth.
“The killer tested a blade here.” Lu’s voice echoed through the basement.
He took out his phone and dialed. It rang three times before someone answered.
“Shen Yu’an, I need you here. The old library basement. I’ll send the address. Bring your examination kit.”

He ended the call, pocketed the phone, and turned to the technical team leader. “Go over the entire basement floor. High-resolution photographs of every inch. Also get the surveillance footage from around this building. See whether anyone has used the fire exit recently.”
Forty minutes later, Shen arrived.

He stepped out of his car carrying his kit, a dark outdoor jacket over his lab coat. The afternoon sun was still fierce. A sheen of sweat covered his forehead, and strands of hair clung to his temples.
“What have we got?” He approached Lu, his voice even.
Lu gave him a brief account. Shen nodded, put on gloves, and crouched beside the scratch.

He took a forensic scale from his kit, placed it beside the mark, and had the scene recorder photograph it. Then he swabbed some of the dark-red staining near the wall, placed the sample in an evidence tube, and screwed on the cap.

“The scratch is about two millimeters deep, with a uniform width. Made by a sharp-edged tool.” Shen spoke just loudly enough for the people beside him to hear. “The tool characteristics match the scratch inside the granite cavity at the sculpture park.”
He stood, walked halfway around the basement, then crouched beside the blurred shoe prints and shone his flashlight across them at an angle.
“The tread pattern is incomplete, but the direction of heel wear is similar to the size forty-one print from the factory.”
The technical team leader wrote rapidly beside him.
Shen crouched on the floor, his gaze passing over every inch of dust. His movements were slow and steady, as though he were admiring a painting.
Of course he knew how the scratch had been made.

Two weeks earlier, he had tested a blade here. It was the same type of scalpel blade he had used in the crime. He had drawn it across the concrete wall seven times. The angle had been wrong on the first six attempts; only the seventh had felt natural. The dark-red stains came from a trial he had performed on a stray cat. He had found it in the back alley, thin as a bundle of bones, strangled it, and brought it into the basement. The placement and angle of every cut had followed the intended procedure.
The whole process had taken forty minutes. Cleaning the scene had taken an hour and a half.
He stood and brushed the dust from his knees.

“My preliminary assessment is that this was a rehearsal site.” He turned to Lu, his tone that of a routine professional report. “He practiced his cutting angles and the route for moving the body here, then went to the sculpture park once he was satisfied.”
Lu looked at him, his gaze darkening.
“So these weren’t the only two places he scouted.”
“Right.” Shen nodded. “Someone this methodical wouldn’t try only once. The two places we’ve found may be just two entries on his list of alternatives.”
For a few seconds, only the dripping water broke the silence.

Lu’s jaw tightened. He had thought searching the line between the crime scenes might reveal one or two alternatives at most. Now the killer appeared far more cautious than they had anticipated—someone who rehearsed, tested, discarded, and began again, repeatedly.
“Expand the search,” Lu told the officers behind him. “List every abandoned building along this line that meets the criteria. Basements, old factories, empty warehouses. Don’t miss a single one.”
An officer acknowledged the order and went out to make the arrangements.
Shen latched his kit and picked it up. In the dim basement, his face was half in shadow, its expression unreadable.
“Shall I take another set of soil samples?” he asked.
“Yes,” Lu said. “Cross-check them against the factory and the sculpture park. If all three share the same components, he may have used the same transport or lining material.”
When Shen crouched to collect the samples, Lu stood beside him and watched for a while.

The damp air pressed heavily on the chest. A small patch of sweat had soaked through Shen’s clothing and clung to his shoulder blades. His sampling movements remained steady. His wrist did not tremble, and his breathing had not changed.
“Go upstairs for some air,” Lu said suddenly. “It’s stifling down here.”
Shen’s hands paused for half a second, then continued placing the swab in its evidence tube.
“Nearly finished.”
“Go up first.” Lu left no room for discussion. “The technicians can finish the rest.”
Only then did Shen straighten, remove his gloves, and follow Lu out.

The sunlight outside made them squint. An old street shaded by plane trees ran past the library, its uneven surface lined with parked cars. Lu took a bottle of water from his car and handed it over. Shen accepted it, unscrewed the cap, and drank.
“How’s the shoulder?” Lu leaned against the car door, looking at him.
“All right.” Shen replaced the cap. “It aches a little after crouching down there for so long. It’s better now.”
Lu’s gaze rested on his left shoulder for a second. He said nothing more.
They stood beneath the trees, watching the field officers come and go. The old street was quiet. In the distance, a scrap collector’s loudspeaker repeated its flat little tune.
“Where do you think he’ll strike next?” Lu asked suddenly.
Shen turned to look at him.

He did not need to think about the answer. The next ritual’s location was already settled: the old waterworks in the south of the city, somewhere he had scouted five times and checked every surveillance blind spot. The window was eight days away. That night there would be a total lunar eclipse, and the city’s nighttime brightness would be thirty percent lower than usual.
But his expression hesitated by exactly the right amount, as though he were considering the question seriously.

“Hard to say.” He turned the water bottle halfway around in his hand. “His selection criteria are consistent—concealment, no camera coverage, a structure suitable for hiding a body. You could count the places in An’an that meet them on two hands. Screening for those features should narrow it down.”
Lu nodded, looking toward the end of the street.
“I’ll have them check every abandoned building in the city.”
Shen did not answer. He leaned against the car door and looked at a crack in the road.
A weed had pushed through it, wilting in the sun.

He was making another calculation. Lu was half a day ahead of his estimate. Shen had intended never to return to the old library after rejecting it, yet the police had still unearthed it. Fortunately, he had cleaned the basement thoroughly. The cat’s body was long gone. Only scratches and shoe prints remained. Even if those matched, they could prove only that someone had been there, not who.
The risk was manageable.
What required real care was the next eight days.
Six that evening. Lu’s office.

Two more red circles had appeared on the whiteboard—the old library basement and the abandoned swimming pool. Linked with the sculpture park and the machine-tool factory, the four sites formed an irregular diamond. At its center lay an old residential neighborhood awaiting demolition.
Lu stood at the board with a marker in his hand and tapped the demolition area with a fingertip.
“Here.” He turned toward the key officers gathered around the desk. “All the places the killer scouted lie inside this diamond. His range of activity stays within it.”
The technical team leader leaned closer. “You think he lives nearby?”
“Not necessarily.” Lu marked an X over the demolition area. “But at the very least, he knows every alley and every camera in this neighborhood. An outsider couldn’t know it this well.”
The room was silent for a few seconds.

The female officer from the canvassing team consulted her notebook. “Mostly elderly people live in this part of the old city. The young residents moved out long ago. The demolition notice has been up for six months, but work hasn’t started. It’s fine during the day. At night, it’s pitch-black. There aren’t even any streetlights.”

“Then start there.” Lu set down the marker. “Door to door. Find out whether there have been any new tenants in the last three months, anyone coming and going in the middle of the night, anyone loitering nearby. Focus on unemployed men living alone who have a medical background.”
The officers noted the instructions and began to leave.
Shen sat in a corner chair, turning a pen in his hand. He had said nothing throughout.
Only when most of them had gone did he rise and pick up his kit.
“I’ll take today’s samples over to the laboratory.”
“Mm.” Lu sorted the papers on his desk without looking up. “No overtime tonight. Go home early.”
Shen acknowledged him and went out.
The corridor was empty, the overhead lights humming. He walked to the elevators, pressed the down button, and took out his phone while he waited.
No new messages.
He pocketed it again. The doors opened, and he stepped inside and pressed B1.
When he drove out of the bureau gates, the evening rush had just ended. There were fewer cars than during the day. He followed his familiar route until a red light stopped him at a crossroads.
A black sedan waited in the next lane, its window half-open.
Shen glanced across casually and met the driver’s eyes.
The man was in his thirties, with a crew cut, a faint scar on his chin, and a dark-gray T-shirt. He looked at Shen without any change of expression, as though at an ordinary passerby.
The light turned green.
The black sedan moved first, joining the traffic. Shen followed at a normal distance.

Three intersections later, the sedan turned into an alley. Shen did not follow. He continued along the main road, made a U-turn at the next lights, and returned to his apartment complex by another route.
He parked in the garage and stayed in the driver’s seat, tapping the steering wheel twice.
Crew cut. Scar on the chin.

He knew the man. Codename: the Pruner. An operative responsible for the organization’s cleanups and loose ends. Two ranks above Shen. He did not ordinarily take part in rituals; he stepped in only when something needed putting in order afterward.
His presence in An’an meant the people above had begun to take an interest in the progress of this game.
Shen opened the door, got out, locked the car, and entered the elevator.
The mirror reflected his face, still wearing its usual expressionless look.
The Pruner’s arrival was not good news. Sending one of their own to watch meant the higher ranks had high expectations for this game—high enough to require someone on the ground to confirm them.
His performance would have to become more convincing.
At home, he dropped his kit in the entrance hall and went to the kitchen for a glass of water. As he lifted it to his lips, he stopped.
The hallucinations had returned.
This time it was a man’s voice, very low, speaking close to his ear: “Don’t give yourself away.”
Without expression, Shen drank the water and set the glass in the sink.
He went to the window and lifted a corner of the curtain.
A black sedan stood beneath the streetlight at the entrance to the complex. Dark film covered its windows. He could not tell whether anyone was inside.
The Pruner.
He let the curtain fall and turned toward the bathroom.
He switched on the hot water. Steam rose around him. He stood beneath the shower with his eyes closed, the water striking his head and drowning out most of the phantom voice.
The game had only reached its midpoint. He still had enough cards to play.

alt.en: Lu Zheng and Shen Yu’an examine scratches in the dusty basement of the abandoned library.
alt.zh: 陆峥与沈予安在废弃图书馆地下室勘验灰尘中的划痕。

zh: 第四天上午，走访组在拆迁区摸到一条新线索。
陆峥接到电话的时候正在办公室吃泡面，塑料叉子插在半开的纸桶里，汤面上浮着一层油花。电话那头的女警声音压得很低，背景里有老式风扇吱呀转动的声响。
"陆队，三号院三号楼的张奶奶说，她上周三凌晨起来上厕所，透过窗户看见楼下巷子里走过一个人。男的，个子不高，穿一身黑，走路没声音。她当时没在意，以为是隔壁楼的住户出来倒垃圾。"
陆峥把泡面搁在桌角。"她看清脸了吗。"
"没有。三楼往下看，大半夜的，只能看见个轮廓。但她记住一个细节——那人手里拎着个方形的东西，用黑布裹着，看形状像个画框。"
画框。
陆峥的眉头动了一下。
两起仪式命案的现场都有构图特征，凶手对画面感的追求近乎偏执。如果他在踩点的时候随身带着画框之类的东西用来模拟构图比例，那这个人的行事风格比预估的还要极端。
"还有别的吗。"
"张奶奶说那人走得特别慢，走两步就停下来站一会儿，像在找什么东西。她看了大概有五分钟，那人拐进巷子尽头就没影了。"
巷子尽头是一堵塌了一半的围墙，围墙后面是废弃游泳馆的后院。
陆峥挂了电话，抓起椅背上的外套往外走。经过办公区的时候，他扫了一眼，沈予安的工位空着，白搭在椅背上。
"小周，沈法医呢。"
旁边一个年轻警员抬头。"一早就去检验科了，说今天要把旧图书馆采的那批样本出初检报告。"
陆峥点头，脚步没停，径直出了大门。
废弃游泳馆的后院比想象中更荒。
铁丝网围栏倒了大半，里面长满了半人高的野草，地面上散落着碎砖和旧建筑材料。后院东边就是游泳馆的主体建筑，外墙贴着白色瓷砖，大片脱落，露出里面灰黑色的水泥底子。入口处挂着一把生锈的铁链锁，锁芯已经被人撬开过，挂扣歪在一边。
陆峥蹲在围墙根底下，手指拨开杂草。
泥地上有几枚鞋印，被雨水泡过，边缘模糊，但还能辨认出鞋底纹路。他用比例尺贴上去比了一下，掏出手机拍照。
"和旧图书馆的鞋印能对上吗。"他问旁边的技术员。
技术员蹲下来看了两眼，摇头。"纹路不一样，这个鞋印底纹更深，像是工装靴。"
机床厂那枚四十一码运动鞋印，旧图书馆那枚模糊鞋印，现在后院这枚工装靴印。三双鞋，三个尺码。
陆峥站起身，目光扫过整个后院。
张奶奶说那个人走两步停一步，像在找东西。如果凶手真的在这里模拟过构图，那他选的观察点一定有讲究。他绕着后院走了半圈，在西北角停住了。
这里位置最高，站在这个点上，视线可以穿过铁丝网，同时看见游泳馆正门、后院出口和三条巷子的岔路口。
他蹲下去看地面。
草被人踩倒过一片，面积不大，刚好够一个人站着不动。踩倒的草茎已经发黄，说明留下痕迹的时间有几天了。
"取样。"陆峥站起身，"这个位置采一组足迹，再看看有没有烟头、纸巾之类的遗留物。"
技术员立刻忙活起来。
陆峥掏出手机拨沈予安的号码。响了四声被接起来，那边背景安静，应该是在检验科。
"后院西北角，过来看看。"
"好，我二十分钟到。"
电话挂了。陆峥把手机揣回兜里，靠在断墙上点了根烟。八月的太阳已经很毒了，晒在后脖颈上发烫，野草被晒出一股青涩的苦味。他吐了口烟，目光落在游泳馆黑洞洞的入口上。
二十分钟后，沈予安到了。
他从车上下来的时候手里拎着勘验箱，白大褂外面套了件薄外套，额角有汗。走到陆峥面前，他先朝后院四周扫了一圈，然后才开口。
"什么情况。"
陆峥把张奶奶的目击线索和发现的踩痕讲了一遍。沈予安听完，点点头，戴上手套，蹲到西北角那片踩倒的草前面。
他从箱子里取出手电，侧着光照地面。灰尘上有几个模糊的足印，深度很浅，看得出来站的时间不长。
"站位很讲究。"沈予安的声音不高，"这个角度能同时覆盖三个方向。他在这里观察过很久。"
他站起身，走到游泳馆入口前面，仰头看了看那扇歪着的铁链锁。
"锁是新撬的。"他伸手指了指锁扣上的断口，"金属断面发亮，没有锈。"
陆峥凑过来看了一眼，确实如此。断口上还能看到新鲜的金属光泽，和旁边那些积了多年灰的旧痕迹完全不同。
"进去看看。"
两人推开门，里面一股霉味扑面而来。游泳馆的大池子早就干了，池底积着厚厚的灰尘和碎玻璃，水面上曾经标注的深浅刻度还依稀可见，红蓝油漆剥落得斑斑驳驳。看台的塑料座椅缺了大半，剩下的也裂了口子，上面落满灰尘和鸟粪。
沈予安沿着池边走，脚步放得很慢。他的目光从池底扫到看台，又从看台扫到天花板的钢架结构。
"这里空间够高。"他开口，"如果藏尸的话，钢架上面有一层检修通道，宽度大概八十公分，躺一个人绰绰有余。"
陆峥顺着他指的方向抬头看。确实，泳池上方四五米高的位置，有一圈环绕整个场馆的金属检修通道，被灰尘和阴影盖着，不仔细看很难发现。
"上去看看。"
检修通道的梯子在馆内东南角，铁梯子锈得厉害，踩上去咯吱响。陆峥先爬，沈予安跟在后面。爬到一半的时候，上面的铁锈渣子掉下来，落在沈予安手背上，他没躲，继续往上爬。
通道比想象中窄，两个人并排走不开，只能一前一后。灰尘厚得踩出脚印，陆峥走在前面，每一步都留下清晰的鞋印。
走了大概十米，陆峥停住了。
前面的灰尘上，有一片被蹭过的痕迹。
不是鞋印，是一种长条状的擦痕，像有人把什么东西沿着通道推过去。擦痕旁边还落了几片干枯的玫瑰花瓣，白得发灰，黏在灰尘里。
陆峥蹲下去，没碰花瓣。
"叫技术员上来。"
沈予安站在他身后，低头看着那几片花瓣。
他当然知道花瓣为什么会在这里。三天前他上来过一次，实地测量检修通道的宽度和承重，确认能放下一具成年人的遗体。当时他带了一小束白玫瑰做模拟摆放，走的时候漏了三片在角落里。
他以为已经捡干净了。
看来那天夜里光线不好，有三片粘在灰尘里没看见。
"花瓣残留和前两个现场的品种一致。"沈予安的声音平稳得没有一丝波澜，"建议取样比对。"
陆峥回头看了他一眼。
阳光从游泳馆高处的破窗斜射进来，在通道上切出一道光柱，灰尘在光柱里翻飞。沈予安站在光柱边缘，半张脸在光里，半张脸在阴影里，表情专注而冷静，像在看任何一个普通现场。
陆峥收回目光，掏出对讲机叫技术员上来。
从游泳馆出来已经是中午。
日头最毒的时候，柏油路被晒得发软，空气里有一股热浪扭曲的味道。陆峥拉开车门，从副驾上拿了两瓶水，递了一瓶给沈予安。
沈予安接过来，拧开喝了一口。
"你觉得他下一次会选哪里。"陆峥靠在车门上，拧着瓶盖问。
沈予安用手背蹭了一下额角的汗，目光扫过游泳馆周围的街道。
"检修通道能藏人，空间够高，监控盲区。"他顿了顿，"符合他的所有标准。但这里已经被我们找到了，他不会再用。"
"所以他在这个菱形范围里，还有别的备选点。"
陆峥把水瓶盖拧上，眉骨压得很低。他原本以为找到旧图书馆和游泳馆这两个点，包围圈已经够小了。现在看来，凶手的备选清单上至少还有三到四个位置。
"走访组今天把这片老城区翻一遍。"陆峥拉开车门，"挨家挨户问，最近半个月有没有见过陌生人在附近转悠。你呢，下午回检验科出报告？"
"嗯。"沈予安拉开车门坐进去，"花瓣比对结果出来我第一时间告诉你。"
两辆车先后驶离游泳馆。
沈予安开着自己的灰色轿车，沿着原路回市局。等红灯的时候，他从后视镜里扫了一眼。
后面没有那辆黑色轿车。
修剪匠没有跟。这说明对方只是在监视，还没到需要贴身盯梢的程度。
他转了个弯，把车开进市局大院。停好车，坐在驾驶座上没动，手指在方向盘上敲了两下。
三片花瓣。
这是个失误。
他做事情从来不留这种尾巴。那天晚上在检修通道上，他戴着头灯模拟了二十分钟花瓣摆放位置，走的时候从头到尾检查了两遍。三片花瓣粘在灰尘缝里，头灯角度没照到，成了漏网之鱼。
好在只是花瓣。花瓣只能证明"有人来过"，证明不了"是谁"。检验科做成分比对，结果只会是"和前两起现场的白玫瑰品种一致"，进一步强化"同一凶手"的判断——而这一点，警方本来就已经知道了。
不影响大局。
他推开车门下了车，拎着勘验箱走进大楼。
走廊里遇到技术组长，对方抱着一摞打印纸，看见他就停下来。
"沈法医，旧图书馆那批泥土样本初筛出来了，和机床厂的土壤成分重合度百分之八十二。"
"花瓣上的机油残留呢。"
"正在做质谱，下午能出结果。"
沈予安点头，继续往前走。推开检验科的门，里面空荡荡的，只有一个化验员趴在实验台前看显微镜。他把勘验箱放在自己工位上，脱下外套挂好，坐下来打开电脑。
屏幕亮起来，桌面上是赵强的尸检照片文件夹。他点开最后一张照片，那是死者胸腔内部的特写，脏器上的锐器创口清晰可见。
他盯着那张照片看了两秒，面无表情地关掉了。
接下来八天，他需要做的事情很明确：正常上班，正常出报告，正常配合陆峥的所有调查，正常扮演那个沉稳可靠的法医。同时在脑子里把下一场仪式的每一个细节再过一遍——踩点路线、运输工具、藏尸位置、花瓣数量、清理流程。
不能再出三片花瓣这种纰漏。
下午三点，化验室的机油残留结果出来了。沈予安拿着报告单走到陆峥办公室，敲门进去。
陆峥正在白板前写东西，听见声音回过头。
"机油成分和机床厂地面残留的一致。"沈予安把报告单放在桌上，"说明运输尸体的工具经过机床厂，或者铺垫材料沾过那里的机油。"
陆峥拿起报告单扫了一眼，放下。
"走访组那边有消息了。"他指了指白板上新贴的一张照片，"这片老城区的巷口小卖部老板说，上周二晚上十一点多，见过一个穿黑衣服的人在对面站了半小时，手里拿着个相机一样的东西对着游泳馆方向拍。"
照片是小卖部监控截的，画质很差，画面里只有一个模糊的人影站在路灯底下，肩膀上挎着个包，脸完全看不清。
"相机。"陆峥的指尖点在照片上，"他在记录自己的构图。"
沈予安看着那张模糊的监控截图，表情没什么变化。
那不是相机。是一个小型水平仪，用来测量花瓣摆放的水平角度。小卖部老板隔着一条街，黑灯瞎火的，把水平仪认成了相机。
"要不要把这个截图发悬赏。"沈予安问。
"发了。"陆峥摇头，"画质太差，脸都没有，发出去也没用。"
他转过身，靠在办公桌边上，目光落在沈予安脸上。
"这两天跟着跑现场，肩膀没事吧。"
沈予安的表情恰到好处地松了一点，像被这个问题问得有点无奈。"真没事，就是昨天在地下室蹲久了酸了一会儿。"
陆峥看了他两秒，没再说什么，从抽屉里拿出一个小药盒递过来。
"活血化瘀的药膏，回去抹一下。"
沈予安接过来，药盒还带着抽屉里的温度。他低头看了一眼，又抬头看向陆峥。
"谢了陆队。"
"下班早点走。"陆峥转回去面对白板，"今天不用守着了。"
沈予安把药膏揣进口袋，推门出去。
走廊里灯光惨白，他站在门口，低头看了一眼手里的药盒。白色塑料壳，上面印着三个字，是药店最常见的那种舒筋活血膏。
他拉开药盒盖子，挤了一点药膏在指尖，随便在虎口上抹了抹。
药膏凉丝丝的，气味冲得很。
他把药盒盖好，塞进白大褂口袋深处，转身走向检验科。
窗外的天色开始暗下来，夕阳把大楼的影子拉得很长。办公区里键盘声不停，没人注意到法医办公室的灯已经灭了一盏。
沈予安坐在工位上，面前摊着一张空白的勘查记录表。他拿起笔，在表格最上面一栏写下日期，字迹工整，力道均匀。
八天。
他在心里数着。
月全食那天晚上，城南老自来水厂的蓄水池顶部，刚好有一个完美的圆形平台。直径四米，四周无遮挡，从下面仰望只能看见天空。白玫瑰铺满整个平台边缘，遗体摆放在圆心位置，花瓣按照对称纹路层层铺开。
从下面抬头看上去，像一轮从井底升起来的月亮。
他写完日期，把笔搁下，靠在椅背上闭了一会儿眼。
幻听又来了，这次是一段节奏很快的鼓点，像某种仪式的配乐。他从口袋里摸出药瓶，倒出两片，干咽下去。
鼓点慢慢退了。
窗外最后一点天光也沉下去了。市局大楼的灯一盏盏亮起来，像棋盘上落子的坐标。
他睁开眼，拿起笔，继续填表。
第五天早上八点，陆峥到办公室的时候，技术组的人已经熬了一整夜。
办公区的灯全亮着，白板上又贴了三张监控截图，都是从老城区各个巷口调出来的。画面里都是凌晨的空巷子，路灯昏黄，偶尔有一只野猫窜过。警员们趴在桌上补觉，显示器上的录像还在循环播放，蓝光映着一张两张疲惫的脸。
技术组长从工位上抬起头，眼睛里全是血丝，手里捏着半杯凉透的咖啡。
"陆队，有发现。"
陆峥把外套搭在椅背上，走过去。
技术组长点了一下鼠标，屏幕上的录像暂停在一帧画面上。凌晨两点十七分，巷口监控拍下来的画面里，一个穿深色连帽衫的人推着一辆手拉车站在路灯底下。手拉车上面盖着一块黑布，布的形状鼓鼓囊囊，看大小像一个长方形的箱子。
"这个人从巷子东口进来，推着车往西走，速度很慢。"技术组长拖动进度条，画面里的人影一步步往前挪，"走到游泳馆后院围墙那个位置停了大概四分钟，然后继续往西，从西口出去。西口外面的监控坏了半个月了，跟丢了。"
"能看清脸吗。"
"帽檐压得太低，正脸一个像素都没有。身高大概一米七五到一米七八，体型偏瘦。"
陆峥盯着屏幕上那个模糊的人影。
手拉车。盖着黑布。凌晨两点十七分。
和雕塑公园保安描述的那个"穿黑色连帽卫衣、身形偏瘦、走路很稳"的人，轮廓对上了。
"时间对得上。"陆峥的手指在桌面上敲了两下，"赵强的死亡时间是凌晨一点到两点。他推着尸体从机床厂出来，经过游泳馆后院，再运到雕塑公园。这条路刚好把三个点串起来了。"
"我们也是这么判断的。"技术组长又点开另一张截图，"另外，走访组从机床厂旁边的废品站问到一个夜班老头，说那天凌晨三点多听见外面有手拉车轱辘碾过石子的声音。他探头看了一眼，街上空的，只看见远处有个黑影拐进了主路。"
陆峥拉过椅子坐下来，把两段监控录像从头到尾又看了一遍。
推车的人步速很稳，肩膀没有负重后该有的歪斜。一个人推着装成年人尸体的手拉车，凌晨三点走在空无一人的巷子里，步速和散步差不多。
心理素质好得反常。
"拉一张模拟画像。"陆峥站起身，"身高一米七五到一米七八，体型偏瘦，穿连帽衫。发到各派出所协查，重点查老城区周边最近租过手拉车的人。"
技术组长记下指令，转头去安排。
陆峥走到白板前面，把游泳馆后院的位置又圈了一遍。现在四个点——雕塑公园、机床厂、旧图书馆、游泳馆后院——全部落在了一个直径三公里的圈子里。凶手的活动范围就在这个圈里，他熟悉每一条巷子、每一个监控盲区。
剩下的问题是，这个人到底住在哪，或者说，他的落脚点在哪。
办公室门被推开，沈予安走进来。
他今天穿了一件浅灰色短袖，外面套着白大褂，手里端着一个马克杯。杯子里冒着热气，是咖啡。走到自己工位上放下东西，他才注意到白板上新增的监控截图。
"这么早。"他走过来，目光落在屏幕上那帧手拉车的画面。
"技术组刚调出来的。"陆峥把情况简要讲了一遍。沈予安听完，凑近屏幕看了两秒。
"手拉车。"他重复了一遍这个词，"运输工具选得很讲究。这种车在老城区到处都是，废品站、小卖部、菜市场都有，丢了也没人报警。"
"而且黑布盖着，大半夜的从外面看，和废品站拉货的没区别。"沈予安端起马克杯喝了一口，"就算被监控拍下来，也不会有人多看一眼。"
陆峥看了他一眼。这话在理，和技术组昨晚的分析结论完全一致。
"检验科那边有结果了吗。"陆峥问。
"花瓣上的机油成分和机床厂地面残留的一致，报告刚打出来。"沈予安从白大褂口袋里抽出一张纸递过去，"另外，旧图书馆地下室那点暗红色污渍，血型做出来了，是O型。和赵强的血型吻合。"
陆峥接过报告扫了一眼，放在桌上。
旧图书馆确实是预演点。暗红色污渍不是猫的，是他试刀的时候从赵强身上溅上去的？不对——赵强的尸体一直在机床厂处理，旧图书馆只是试刀。那暗红色污渍是哪来的？
他抬眼看沈予安。
沈予安已经转身走回自己工位了，正低头翻着一摞文件，神情专注，和平时没什么两样。
陆峥把这个念头压下去。O型血的人多了去了，暗红色污渍也可能是老鼠、野猫之类的动物血。检验科只是做了血型初筛，DNA结果还得等几天。
上午十点，网安组那边来了消息。
陆峥下楼走进网安办公室的时候，满屋子都是服务器运转的嗡嗡声。十几台显示器并排摆着，屏幕上滚动着密密麻麻的代码和数据曲线。网安组组长是个戴眼镜的年轻人，头顶发量堪忧，看见陆峥进来，推了推眼镜。
"陆队，那个暗网活跃ID又发帖了。"
他把屏幕转过来。
帖子是英文的，发在La Rose Éternelle的加密板块里，发布时间是今天凌晨四点。内容很短，配了一张图。
图是一张黑白摄影，拍的是一个圆形平台，平台边缘摆着一圈花。构图对称，光线昏暗，只看得出来花是白色的。
"这张图。"网安组长放大图片，"我们查了EXIF信息，拍摄地点的GPS坐标被抹掉了，但相机型号是佳能EOS R5。这种相机不便宜，专业级的。"
"帖子内容呢。"
"就一句话。"网安组长指着屏幕，"'The altar is ready.（祭坛已就绪）'"
陆峥盯着那张黑白照片看了很久。
圆形平台。一圈白花。祭坛。
和雕塑公园里的花瓣铺陈是同一个路数，只是这次的构图更完整，更像一个正式的仪式。
"这个发帖ID，能追踪到IP吗。"
"还是老样子，七层代理，洋葱路由，真实出口在境外。"网安组长摇头，"但我们发现一个新情况。这个ID最近三天的登录时间，全部集中在凌晨两点到四点之间。"
陆峥的眉头动了一下。
凌晨两点到四点。赵强的死亡时间是凌晨一点到两点。两起命案的作案时间窗口，都在这个时段之内。
凶手习惯在深夜行动。发帖时间和作案时间重叠，说明他发完帖没多久就动手，或者刚动手完就上来记录。
"把这个时间段记下来。"陆峥指着屏幕，"以后这个ID一上线就报警。"
"已经设了。"
陆峥走出网安办公室，走廊里的冷气开得很足。他站在电梯口等电梯，脑子里把所有线索过了一遍。
四个案发相关点，一个运输工具，一个暗网ID，一个发帖时间段。所有碎片都在慢慢拼合，但核心的那块——凶手到底是谁——还是空白。
电梯到了，他走进去按了三楼。
三楼是检验科和法医办公室。他推开沈予安办公室的门，里面没人。隔壁解剖室的灯亮着，隔着玻璃能看见里面有人影在动。
陆峥走过去，隔着玻璃敲了敲门。
沈予安正在解剖台旁边填记录，听见声音回过头，看见是陆峥，摘下口罩走出来。
"怎么了。"
"网安那边刚截到一个帖子。"陆峥把手机递过去，屏幕上是那张黑白照片的翻拍，"圆形平台，白花，写着'祭坛已就绪'。"
沈予安接过手机，低头看了一眼。
他的目光在照片上停了两秒。
这张照片他见过。三天前他自己拍的。那天深夜他一个人爬上老自来水厂的蓄水池顶部，用佳能EOS R5拍了二十多张，选了这张最好的发给组织。照片里的圆形平台就是蓄水池顶部，边缘那圈白花是他提前摆上去做效果测试的样例。
他没想到组织会把这张照片发到公开板块里。
"祭坛。"沈予安把手机递回去，语气平静，"和雕塑公园那次的花瓣铺陈是同一个路数。圆形构图，对称，仪式感很强。"
"你觉得这是预告？"
"有可能。"沈予安把口罩塞进口袋，"他在展示下一场仪式的地点。圆形平台，白花，说明下一个现场会比之前的更讲究。"
陆峥把手机收回来，屏幕暗下去。
"照片里那个圆形平台，你能认出来是哪吗。"
沈予安又低头看了一眼——这次是演的。他皱着眉，像在认真辨认。
"看不出来。背景全黑，没有参照物。圆形平台这种结构，安市能找到的地方不少。水塔、蓄水池、圆形广场、旧建筑穹顶……太多了。"
陆峥点头。他自己也认不出来。
"我让人把这张图下发给各辖区，让民警排查一下有没有符合这个特征的地点。"
"好。"沈予安应了一声，转身走回解剖室，"我这边还有两具无名尸的记录要补，先走了。"
门带上了。
陆峥站在走廊里，看着玻璃门后面那个穿解剖服的背影重新回到手术台旁边，低下头继续记录。
他转身往电梯口走。
晚上九点，办公楼里的人走得差不多了。
陆峥的办公室还亮着灯。桌上摊着老城区的地图，上面用红笔标了十几个点，都是技术组排查出来的"符合圆形平台特征"的位置。蓄水池、水塔、圆形花坛、废弃天文台、旧体育馆穹顶……一个一个看过去，符合条件的有七八个，全部派人去摸了，目前都没有新发现。
门被敲了两下。
沈予安站在门口，手里拎着两个便利店的袋子。
"路过楼下，顺手买了点吃的。"他走进来，把一个袋子放在陆峥桌上，"饭团，还有牛奶。"
陆峥抬头看了他一眼。袋子是温的，饭团还带着微波过的热度。
"你怎么还没走。"
"记录补完就走，看见你办公室灯还亮着。"沈予安靠在办公桌边上，目光扫过桌上摊开的地图，"还在排查圆形平台？"
"七个点全跑了一遍，都没发现。"陆峥拆开饭团包装，咬了一口，"照片里的平台到底在哪。"
沈予安的视线落在地图上，手指在其中一个位置点了一下。
"城南老自来水厂。"
陆峥抬眼。
"那里有个蓄水池顶部，圆形的，直径大概四米。"沈予安的语气像在随口提供线索，"我去年出过一次那边的现场，一个流浪汉冻死在里面。上去过，顶上确实是个圆形平台，周围无遮挡。"
陆峥的筷子停了一下。
他盯着沈予安的脸。对方的表情很自然，像在回忆一个普通的旧案。
"你怎么不早说。"
"之前没想到。"沈予安耸了耸肩，"今天看见你在这儿画圈，才突然想起来那个地方。"
陆峥把嘴里的饭团咽下去，拿起电话拨外勤组。
"明天一早，去城南老自来水厂。对，蓄水池顶部，排查。"
挂了电话，他看向沈予安。
"谢了。"
"应该的。"沈予安直起身，"我先走了，你也早点回去。"
他拉开门走出去，脚步声在空旷的走廊里渐渐远了。
陆峥坐在椅子上，把最后一口饭团吃完，喝了口牛奶。牛奶是温的，甜的。
他低头看地图上那个被沈予安点过的位置——城南老自来水厂。如果那里真的是下一个现场，那他明天一早过去，应该能找到踩点痕迹。
他不知道的是，此刻走出大楼的沈予安，正站在停车场的灯底下，掏出手机。
屏幕上没有新消息。
他把手机揣回兜里，拉开车门坐进去。驾驶座的后视镜里，市局大楼的灯光一扇一扇灭下去，他办公室那盏最后暗了。
沈予安发动车子，驶出停车场。
他主动给陆峥递了城南老自来水厂这个地点。
这步棋走得险。按照陆峥的刑侦速度，明天一早过去排查，大概率能在蓄水池附近找到他踩点时留下的微弱痕迹——他上周三在那里待了两个小时，测量平台尺寸、试摆花瓣、清理地面，虽然戴了手套鞋套，但灰尘上总会留下点什么。
但他必须这么做。
修剪匠在监视。上层要看的是一场完美的游戏——警方一步步逼近，又一次次扑空，最后在仪式完成的那一刻才恍然大悟。如果他不主动"提供线索"，陆峥的排查方向就会偏掉，游戏的节奏就乱了。
他需要陆峥朝着正确的方向走，但永远慢他一步。
明天警方去老自来水厂排查，会发现踩点痕迹，会加强那片区域的布控。然后呢？他不会在那里动手。他会换一个地方。
下一个地点，他已经选好了。
城北废弃天文台的穹顶平台。比自来水厂更高，视野更开阔，圆形结构更完美。月全食那天晚上，从穹顶往下看，整座城市都在脚下，白玫瑰铺满穹顶边缘，正好和天上的月亮形成上下呼应。
蓄水池是故意放出去的烟幕弹。
沈予安开车经过一个十字路口，红灯亮了。他停下来，手指在方向盘上敲了两下。
后视镜里，那辆黑色轿车没有跟来。
修剪匠今天休息。
绿灯亮了，他踩下油门，车子汇入深夜空荡荡的马路。路灯一盏一盏从车顶滑过去，光影在他脸上交替明灭。
他吹了声口哨。
调子是那段幻听里的鼓点旋律，被他用口哨吹得七零八落。
车子拐进小区的时候，门卫室的大爷抬头看了一眼，认出是他，抬杆放行。他把车停进车位，下车，锁门，走进电梯。
电梯镜子里映出他的脸。
嘴角翘着。
他面无表情地把那点弧度压下去，恢复成平时那副冷静淡漠的样子。
门开了，他走出去，掏钥匙开门。
屋里黑着灯，和走的时候一样。他踢掉鞋，走到窗边撩开窗帘一角。
小区门口的路灯底下，空的。
修剪匠今晚没出现。
他放下窗帘，转身走向浴室。热水打开的时候，他站在花洒下面，仰头冲着水流。
八天。
减去今天，还剩七天。
en: On the morning of the fourth day, the canvassing team found a new lead in the demolition area.

Lu was eating instant noodles in his office when the call came. A plastic fork stood in the half-open paper cup, a film of oil floating on the broth. The female officer spoke quietly over the creak of an old electric fan.

“Team Leader Lu, Granny Zhang in Building Three, Courtyard Three, says she got up to use the toilet early last Wednesday morning and saw someone in the alley below her window. A man, not very tall, dressed all in black. He walked without making a sound. She didn’t think much of it—assumed he was someone from the next building taking out the rubbish.”
Lu put the noodles on the corner of his desk. “Did she see his face?”

“No. She was looking down from the third floor in the middle of the night. She could only see an outline. But she remembered one detail: he was carrying something square, wrapped in black cloth. From its shape, she thought it was a picture frame.”
A picture frame.
Lu’s brow shifted.

Both ritual murder scenes showed deliberate composition. The killer’s concern with the visual effect bordered on obsession. If he carried a frame while scouting locations to test the proportions of a composition, his methods were even more extreme than they had estimated.
“Anything else?”

“She says he walked very slowly. Every couple of steps, he stopped and stood still, as if looking for something. She watched for about five minutes. Then he turned at the end of the alley and disappeared.”
