“What brings you here? Didn’t you have a meeting this morning?”
“Postponed.” Lu leaned against the doorframe, watching him.
Shen tied his coat, slender fingers moving, joints clearly defined. Those hands had performed countless autopsies, held scalpels, and tied Lu’s apron.
“How’s your shoulder today?” Lu asked suddenly. “Aching in the rain again?”
Shen’s hands paused for half a second.
“Same as always.” He turned and pressed his left shoulder. “Rub it for me tonight. It’ll be fine.”
His smile was natural, like anyone whose lover had asked about an old injury.
Lu watched. Not a single flaw.
“What do you want for dinner?” Shen lowered his hand and turned to collect his autopsy kit.
“Anything.”
Lu heard none of the morning meeting.

The technical team leader stood at the front discussing Zhou Mingyuan’s questioning, an evidence timeline projected behind him. Lu sat at the end of the table, looking at the eight photographs on the whiteboard.
White Rose. Iris. Daisy. Lily of the Valley. Bauhinia. Camellia. Datura.
Eight flowers.
He reordered their identities in his mind.
Zhou Kun—unemployed, street-level operative.
Su Wan—freelancer, grower.
Old Zheng—flower-shop owner, florist.
Zhou Mingyuan—deputy head of pharmacy, toxin extraction.
Lily of the Valley—logistics dispatcher, transport routes.
Bauhinia—fitness instructor, physical handling.
Lin Zhinuan—retired doctor, intermediary.
Seven people, seven roles. What was missing?
A designer.
Someone capable of devising all these ritual murders. Someone who knew how every scene should be arranged, every flower placed, every incision made.
Someone who understood anatomy and criminal psychology, who could calculate the police response precisely enough to lead an entire municipal criminal investigation team in circles.
Lu tapped the desk once.
That person had stood beside him since the first case.
At every scene, he was there. In every analysis, he took part. He saw every clue first. Before Lu had worked it out, he could even say what the next scene might look like.
Lu remembered Shen crouching beside the body at the sculpture park, looking up to say, “The killer is exceptionally disciplined. He treats murder as an art.”
At the time, Lu had taken it as a forensic physician’s professional judgment.
Now he wondered—how had he known so clearly?
At noon, Lu went alone to the rooftop.
He took out his phone and dialed.
“Hello. I need you to look into someone.”
The person at the other end was a former trainee of his, now working in the provincial public security department’s technical division.
“Who?”
“Shen Yu’an. Lead forensic examiner at the An’an municipal bureau.”
Two seconds of silence. “Your own partner? Why investigate him?”
“Don’t ask.” Lu kept his voice low. “I want his complete background. Birth certificate, education, employment, entry and exit records, bank transactions. As detailed as possible.”
“Team Leader Lu, are you…”
“Do it.”
He hung up and stood at the rooftop’s edge.
The wind snapped his jacket. An’an spread below him, dense buildings like a concrete forest.
He told himself it was only a check. Nine members, eight arrested. Any detective would examine everyone around him while seeking the last. Shen was only one of them.
Nothing more.
Three days later, his former trainee sent the material.
Lu sat in his office and read it piece by piece.

Shen Yu’an, twenty-six, native of An’an. Father died early, mother remarried, raised by his maternal grandmother. Combined undergraduate and master’s program in forensic medicine at a medical university. Joined the bureau directly after graduation. A record as clean as blank paper.
Entry and exit records: two trips. Japan after university graduation, Hong Kong for an academic conference last year.
Bank records: monthly salary, modest expenses, rent and food, occasional clothes. No unusual large deposits.
Social connections: almost none. Colleagues called him quiet and diligent. Few friends; most WeChat contacts related to work.
Clean. Too clean.
Lu closed the file and leaned back.
An orphan, no family, no social ties, no leverage against him. Someone ideally suited to hiding anywhere.
He shook his head.
What was happening to him? He was growing paranoid.
When he came home that evening, Shen sat on the living-room rug opening a parcel.
A newly purchased set of dissection blades. The open box held a row of sharp scalpels, flashing coldly beneath the light.
“That’s a lot of blades.” Lu sat beside him.
“The old set went blunt.” Shen lifted one and tested the edge with his thumb. “These are German. Sharp.”
He held the scalpel naturally, fingers around the handle, edge upward, wrist slightly inclined.
Lu watched the grip. Professional. Too professional. Less like a forensic physician examining his tools than a…
He cut off the thought.
“By the way.” Shen looked up suddenly. “The technical team told me Zhou Mingyuan has started talking.”
“Mm?”

“He admitted part of it.” Shen returned the scalpel to its box. “Says he only prepared the drugs. Someone was above him, but he doesn’t know who. All his instructions arrived by encrypted email. They never met.”
Lu looked at him.
“How did you hear that?”
“Xiao Wang from the technical team mentioned it when I brought samples over this afternoon.” Shen tilted his head. “Why?”
“Nothing.”
Shen leaned over and kissed him.
“Don’t think so much. You’ve caught eight. The last one won’t get away.”
His lips were soft, tasting of mint. Lu reached out, held him, and buried his face against his neck.
Shen rested a hand at the back of his head and patted gently.
“It’s all right.” His voice was tender, like someone soothing a child after a nightmare. “It’s over.”
Lu kept his eyes closed.
He breathed in Shen’s scent: disinfectant lingering from his lab coat, shampoo, and something faintly bitter he could not name.
What was it?
He searched his memory. Disinfectant. Formalin. Rust-preventive oil from scalpels.
And a trace of… flowers.
Very faint, almost imperceptible. The scent of black roses.
Lu’s arms tightened.
The person he held was light and warm, his heartbeat steady.
Lu said nothing.
Outside, the night deepened by degrees.

alt.en: Lu Zheng reviews case files at home while Shen Yu’an prepares dinner in the warm kitchen.
alt.zh: 陆峥在家查看案卷，沈予安在暖光中的厨房准备晚餐。

zh: 周明远正式批捕那天，下了一场秋雨。
雨从下午开始下，打在办公室窗户上噼啪响。陆峥坐在桌前，把八个人的案卷全部摊开，一张一张按顺序排好。
白玫瑰周坤。鸢尾苏晚。雏菊老郑。铃兰。紫荆。山茶林知暖。曼陀罗周明远。
八份档案，八张脸，八种花的代号。
他盯着这些名字看了整整一个下午。
技术组长进来送过一次咖啡，看见他这副样子，站在门口犹豫了一下。
"陆队，都批捕了，接下来就是检察院那边的事了。你回去休息吧。"
技术组长带上门出去了。
办公室里只剩下雨声。
陆峥站起身，走到白板前面。
白板上贴了八张照片，围成一个圈。圈的中间，他之前用红笔写了一个大大的问号。
他拿起马克笔，在那个问号旁边，写下组织的全称。
"La Rose Éternelle——永恒玫瑰。"
八个字。
他盯着这行字。
白玫瑰是周坤。鸢尾是苏晚。雏菊是老郑。铃兰。紫荆。山茶。曼陀罗。
八种花，八种植物，全部被警方连根拔起。
花园里的花开了又谢，谢了又开。
那花园的主人呢？
一个花园，不会自己长出来。总得有人播种，有人浇水，有人修剪，有人站在最高处看着一切生长。
这个人叫什么代号？
陆峥的马克笔停在白板上。
他想起林知暖在审讯室里说的那句话——"我就是你们要找的人。"
假的。她不是。她只是被推到台前的挡箭牌。
他想起周明远在审讯室里，怎么都撬不开嘴的样子。他知道上面有人，但他从来没见过那个人。
他想起老郑说的"老太太"，紫荆喊的"夫人"。这些称呼指向的，都是林知暖那个层级。
再往上呢？
再往上，还有一个人。
一个从不出现在任何通讯记录里，从不留下任何痕迹，从不和下面的人直接接触的人。
这个人怎么指挥整个组织？
陆峥的手慢慢放下来。
他转过头，目光落在窗外。雨还在下，城市被雨水模糊成一片光晕。
一个念头像冰水一样从头顶浇下来。
——这个人，根本不需要通过通讯软件指挥。
他就在市局里。
他每天和他们一起开会，一起分析案情，一起追捕自己的手下。他知道警方的每一步动作，知道每一条线索的走向，知道什么时候该抛一个替罪羊，什么时候该故意露一个破绽。
他甚至能在陆峥身边，扮演一个温柔的恋人。
陆峥的手指开始发抖。
他走到桌边，翻开沈予安的那份背景调查。
父亲早逝。母亲改嫁。从小跟着外婆长大。医科大学本硕连读。毕业进市局。
没有异常出入境。没有异常银行流水。没有可疑社会关系。
太干净了。
干净得像一份被精心打磨过的简历。
一个孤儿。一个没有根的人。一个谁都查不出过去的人。
他站在办公室中央，听着外面的雨声。
雨打在窗户上，一下一下，像心跳。
他没有回办公室收拾东西。他抓起外套就往外走。
地下车库，车子发动，轮胎碾过积水路面。雨刷开到最大，前面的路还是模糊的。
他开得很快。闯了一个黄灯，被电子眼拍了都不管。
脑子里翻来覆去只有一个画面——雕塑公园第一次见面，沈予安穿着白大褂走过来，口罩上面露出一双眼睛。
那双眼睛里，什么情绪都没有。
那时候他以为是法医见惯了尸体的冷静。
现在想来——
那是一个猎人，在观察自己的猎物。
车停在小区地下车库。
他坐在车里，没有立刻上去。雨还在下，车库顶上的灯管嗡嗡响，光线惨白。
他掏出手机，翻到沈予安的号码。
通话记录显示，今天下午五点十七分，沈予安给他发过一条消息："今晚做你爱吃的糖醋排骨，早点回来。"
陆峥盯着这条消息看了很久。
他锁了屏，下车，走进电梯。
电梯数字往上跳。十楼。十五楼。二十楼。
叮的一声。
他走出来，掏钥匙，开门。
门开了。
客厅里亮着暖黄的灯。厨房传来抽油烟机的声音，混着糖醋排骨的甜香味。
沈予安站在灶台前面，围着围裙，正在翻锅里的排骨。听见开门声，他回过头，脸上是那个熟悉的、温柔的笑。
"回来了？今天怎么这么晚。"
陆峥站在玄关，没有动。
他看着厨房里的这个人。
灯光从头顶打下来，在他头发上打出一圈浅金。围裙带子在腰后面系了个蝴蝶结。手里拿着锅铲，袖口卷到手肘，露出那截细白的手腕。
这是他住了一年的家。这是他每天抱着睡觉的人。这是他曾经发誓要保护一辈子的人。
"怎么了。"沈予安看见他站着不动，关了火，擦了擦手走过来，"身上都湿了，我给你拿毛巾。"
他走到陆峥面前，伸手想碰他的脸。
陆峥往后退了一步。
沈予安的手停在半空中。
客厅里安静下来。抽油烟机的声音已经关了，只剩下厨房锅里排骨还在滋滋响。
"陆峥？"沈予安的声音有一点疑惑。
陆峥抬起头，看着他。
"你是什么时候开始的。"
沈予安的表情没有变化。"什么什么时候。"
"组织。"陆峥的声音很稳，稳得像结了冰，"La Rose Éternelle。你从什么时候开始的。"
沈予安看着他。
两秒。
他脸上的那个温柔的表情，像面具一样，一点一点卸下来。
不是惊慌。不是被识破后的慌乱。是一种很平静的、终于等到这一刻的释然。
他收回手，转过身，走到沙发旁边坐下来。
动作很自然，像只是听完了一段普通的工作汇报。
"你什么时候知道的。"他问。
声音变了。
不是平时那个温柔的、带着一点撒娇尾音的声音。是一种更冷、更平、不带任何情绪的语调。
陆峥站在原地。
他听到这个声音的时候，心里最后那一点自欺欺人的希望，碎了。
"今天。"陆峥说，"就在办公室。"
沈予安"哦"了一声。他伸手解开围裙的带子，把围裙叠好，放在沙发扶手上。
那个动作太从容了。从容得像在自己家——他本来就是在自己家，这一年来，他每天都在演。
"八个人。"陆峥的声音发紧，"白玫瑰、鸢尾、雏菊、铃兰、紫荆、山茶、曼陀罗。八朵花，全部抓齐了。花园里所有的花都开了。"
他往前走了一步。
"就差一朵。"
沈予安抬起头，看着他。
灯光底下，他的眼睛很平静。没有恐惧，没有愧疚，没有被揭穿后的狼狈。
"黑玫瑰。"陆峥说。
两个字落地。
厨房锅里的排骨还在滋滋响，糖醋的甜味弥漫在整个客厅里。
沈予安靠在沙发上，手臂搭着扶手，姿势松弛。
"你比我想的晚了两周。"他说。
陆峥的手在身侧攥紧了。
"肩伤。"他说，"去年那个逃犯，你替我挡的那一枪。也是设计好的？"
"不是。"沈予安歪了歪头，"那个是真的。我没想到他会掏枪。"
"那你为什么挡。"
"因为如果你死了，"沈予安的语气很平淡，像在解释一个再简单不过的事实，"这个游戏就没法继续了。"
陆峥觉得有什么东西在胸腔里炸开。
游戏。
这一年的同居。接吻。拥抱。每天早上那句"早点回来"。糖醋排骨。肩膀疼了要他揉。下雨天往他怀里钻。
全部是游戏。
"你从来没有……"陆峥的声音卡了一下，"对我有过一点真的？"
沈予安看着他。
他的表情很奇怪。不是残忍，不是得意，是一种近乎好奇的困惑，像在听一个他完全无法理解的问题。
"真的？"他重复了一遍这个词，"陆峥，我是法医。你的尸检报告我都写过，你的骨龄、你的旧伤、你胃里有什么我都知道。你觉得这种关系里，'真的'是什么？"
他站起身，走到窗边。
雨还在下。窗户上蒙着一层水雾。
"你有没有想过，"沈予安的背影对着他，"为什么所有的现场，我都能比你先到？为什么每一次分析，我都能精准地告诉你下一步是什么？为什么周坤、苏晚、老郑、林知暖……一个一个，全部顺着我们布的线，自己走进来？"
陆峥站在原地。
他浑身发冷。
"因为那是我安排的。"沈予安说，"我需要你们抓他们。抓得越多，你越觉得案子在收网。你越觉得快结束了，你就越不会怀疑，那个一直站在你身边帮你破案的人。"
他转过身。
客厅的灯光打在他脸上，那张脸还是那张脸——他爱了一年的脸。但眼睛里的东西完全变了。
没有温柔。没有羞怯。没有依赖。
只有一种冷静的、审视的、像在欣赏一件作品的目光。
"九个核心成员。"沈予安伸出手，掰着手指数，"白玫瑰是我放出来的替罪羊。鸢尾和雏菊是负责种植的。曼陀罗是配药的。铃兰管运输。紫荆管搬运。林知暖是我推出去的挡箭牌。"
他抬起眼。
"八个。全部是我送给你的礼物。"
陆峥的指甲嵌进掌心。
"那你呢。"
"我是黑玫瑰。"沈予安说，"这个组织的创始人。从第一个人到第九个人，全是我挑的。从第一起命案到现在，全部是我设计的。"
他往前走了一步。
"而你，陆队长，"他的声音放轻了，像回到了平时那个温柔的语调里，"是我这一辈子玩过最好的一个游戏。"
厨房的锅里，排骨烧干了。
烟从厨房飘出来，混着糖醋的焦味。两个人都没有动。
陆峥看着眼前这个人。
这一年来，他在这个人身边睡觉，吃饭，接吻，计划着去看海。他以为自己抱住了一个柔软的、需要被保护的人。
他抱住的，是一把刀。
"你从什么时候开始计划这一切的。"陆峥的声音哑了。
"从我进市局第一天。"沈予安说，"面试的时候我就看见你了。你站在走廊那头，跟下属拍桌子。我当时想——这个人，好用。"
"所以你故意进法医室。"
"对。只有站在你身边，我才能知道你的每一步动作。你半夜在哪里布控，你明天要去抓谁，你怀疑到了哪一步——全部在我眼皮底下。"
沈予安走回沙发旁边，拿起那部陆峥再熟悉不过的手机。
他按了两下，屏幕亮了。上面是一串号码，备注是空的。
"周坤被抓的第二天，我发消息给修剪匠，告诉他第三个棋子可以抛了。"沈予安把手机转过来，让陆峥看屏幕，"林知暖进去之前，我亲自给她做的手术，把炸药植进她的脊椎旁边。她以为她在救人，其实她只是我用完就扔的一颗棋子。"
陆峥看着屏幕。
那些他每天看见沈予安在沙发上刷的消息，那些他以为是在和朋友聊天的记录——
全是犯罪指令。
"你报警吧。"沈予安把手机放在茶几上，声音很平，"我不会跑。"
陆峥没有动。
"为什么。"
"因为游戏结束了。"沈予安看着他，眼睛里第一次出现了一点别的东西——不是情绪，是一种完成了作品之后的满足，"八朵花都谢了，花园也该关门了。"
他往前倾了倾身。
"你知道吗，陆峥。这一年我演得真累。早上要害羞，吃饭要撒娇，晚上要往你怀里钻。我有严重的强迫症，我根本不喜欢别人碰我。"
他笑了一下。那个笑容很淡，冷得像玻璃。
"你抱我的时候，我数着你的心跳，数到第一百二十下的时候，你就会睡着。"
陆峥伸出手，摸向腰间。
枪套是空的。他下班的时候把枪锁在办公室保险柜里了。
沈予安看着他的动作，嘴角弯了一下。
"别找了。"他说，"你现在打电话叫人来，我就在这儿坐着。"
窗外的雨还在下。
焦糊味弥漫在客厅里。桌上还摆着两副碗筷，是沈予安晚上多摆的那副。
陆峥掏出手机。
屏幕亮了。他盯着拨号界面，手指悬在上面。
他想起那碗莲藕排骨汤。想起下雨天往他怀里钻的温度。想起那个在他额头上印下的、带着薄荷味的吻。
全部是假的。
他按下了三个数字。
电话接通的那一瞬间，沈予安靠在沙发上，闭上了眼睛。
像一个终于谢幕的演员。
en: An autumn rain fell on the day Zhou Mingyuan’s arrest was formally approved.
It began in the afternoon, pattering against the office window. Lu sat at his desk with all eight case files spread out, arranging them page by page.
White Rose, Zhou Kun. Iris, Su Wan. Daisy, Old Zheng. Lily of the Valley. Bauhinia. Camellia, Lin Zhinuan. Datura, Zhou Mingyuan.
Eight files. Eight faces. Eight flower codenames.
He stared at the names for an entire afternoon.
The technical team leader brought coffee once. Seeing him, he hesitated in the doorway.
“Team Leader Lu, the arrests have all been approved. It’s for the procuratorate now. Go home and rest.”
“Mm.”
The team leader closed the door behind him.
Only the rain remained.
Lu rose and went to the whiteboard.
Eight photographs formed a circle. In its center was the large red question mark he had drawn earlier.
He picked up the marker and wrote the organization’s full name beside it.
“La Rose Éternelle—the Eternal Rose.”
A short line of words.
He stared at it.
White Rose was Zhou Kun. Iris was Su Wan. Daisy was Old Zheng. Lily of the Valley. Bauhinia. Camellia. Datura.
Eight flowers, eight plants, all pulled up by the police.
The garden’s flowers bloomed and withered, withered and bloomed again.
What about the gardener?
A garden could not create itself. Someone had to sow, water, prune, and stand above it all, watching it grow.
What was that person’s codename?
Lu’s marker stopped against the board.
He remembered Lin Zhinuan’s words in the interview room: “I’m the person you’re looking for.”
False. She was not. Only a shield pushed to the front.
He remembered Zhou Mingyuan’s refusal to speak. He knew someone was above him, but had never met that person.
He remembered Old Zheng’s “old lady” and Bauhinia’s “Madam.” Those titles pointed to Lin Zhinuan’s level.
And above that?
Above that, there was someone else.
Someone who never appeared in any communication record, never left a trace, never dealt directly with the people below.
How did this person command the whole organization?
Lu slowly lowered his hand.
He turned toward the window. Rain blurred the city into a haze of light.
A thought washed over him like ice water.
This person did not need messaging software to direct anything.
He was inside the bureau.

Every day, he attended their meetings, analyzed their cases, and pursued his own subordinates alongside them. He knew every police move, every clue’s direction, when to offer a scapegoat, when to expose a deliberate flaw.
He could even stand beside Lu and play a gentle lover.
Lu’s fingers began to shake.
He went to the desk and opened Shen’s background report.
Father died early. Mother remarried. Raised by his grandmother. Combined undergraduate and master’s medical program. Joined the bureau after graduation.
No unusual border crossings. No unusual bank transactions. No suspicious connections.
Too clean.
As clean as a meticulously polished résumé.
An orphan. Someone without roots. Someone whose past no one could uncover.
He stood in the middle of the office, listening to the rain.
It struck the window beat by beat, like a heart.
He did not return to his office to gather his things. He seized his jacket and went out.
Down in the garage, the engine started. Tires rolled through standing water. Even with the wipers at full speed, the road ahead remained blurred.
He drove fast, running a yellow light without caring whether the camera caught him.
One image turned over and over in his mind: their first meeting at the sculpture park, Shen approaching in a white coat, only his eyes visible above the mask.
There had been no emotion in those eyes.
At the time, Lu had assumed it was a forensic physician’s familiarity with death.
Now he understood—
It was a hunter studying his prey.
He parked in the complex’s underground garage.
He remained in the car instead of going straight up. Rain still fell outside. Overhead tubes hummed, casting a sickly white light.
He took out his phone and found Shen’s number.
The call history showed a message sent at 5:17 that afternoon: “Making your favorite sweet-and-sour ribs tonight. Come home early.”
Lu stared at it for a long time.
He locked the screen, got out, and entered the elevator.
The floor numbers rose. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty.
A chime.
He stepped out, took his keys, and unlocked the door.
It opened.
Warm yellow light filled the living room. The kitchen extractor hummed over the sweet scent of ribs.
Shen stood at the stove in an apron, turning the ribs in the pan. At the sound of the door, he looked back with that familiar, gentle smile.
“You’re home? Why so late?”
Lu stood in the entrance without moving.
He looked at the person in the kitchen.
Overhead light edged Shen’s hair in pale gold. His apron was tied in a bow at the back. He held a spatula, sleeves rolled to his elbows, those slender pale wrists exposed.
This was the home Lu had lived in for a year. The person he held every night. The person he had sworn to protect for the rest of his life.
“What’s wrong?” Seeing him motionless, Shen switched off the stove, wiped his hands, and approached. “You’re soaked. I’ll get a towel.”
He came up to Lu and reached for his face.
Lu stepped back.
Shen’s hand stopped in midair.
The living room fell quiet. The extractor had stopped. Only the ribs still sizzled in the kitchen pan.
“Lu Zheng?” A little puzzlement entered Shen’s voice.
Lu raised his head and looked at him.
“When did you start?”
Shen’s expression did not change. “Start what?”
“The organization.” Lu’s voice was steady, frozen solid. “La Rose Éternelle. When did you start it?”
Shen looked at him.
Two seconds.
The gentle expression came away little by little, like a mask being removed.
No panic. No alarm at being discovered. Only a quiet release, as though this moment had finally arrived.
He lowered his hand, turned, and sat beside the sofa.
The movement was natural, as though he had merely heard an ordinary work report.
“When did you know?” he asked.
His voice had changed.
Not the familiar tenderness with its faintly coaxing inflection. This was colder, flatter, without emotion.
Lu stood where he was.
At that voice, the last self-deceiving fragment of hope inside him broke.
“Today,” Lu said. “In the office.”
“Oh.” Shen untied his apron, folded it neatly, and placed it on the sofa arm.
He was too composed. As though in his own home—which, of course, he was. Every day for the past year, he had been acting.
“Eight people.” Lu’s voice tightened. “White Rose, Iris, Daisy, Lily of the Valley, Bauhinia, Camellia, Datura. Eight flowers. All caught. Every flower in the garden has bloomed.”
He took a step forward.
“Except one.”
Shen raised his head.
Under the light, his eyes were calm. No fear, no guilt, no humiliation at being exposed.
“Black Rose,” Lu said.
The words fell between them.
The ribs still sizzled in the kitchen. Their sweet-and-sour fragrance filled the room.
Shen leaned back, an arm resting loosely on the sofa.
“You took two weeks longer than I expected,” he said.
Lu’s hand clenched at his side.
“The shoulder wound,” he said. “That fugitive last year. The bullet you took for me. Was that planned too?”
“No.” Shen tilted his head. “That was real. I didn’t expect him to draw a gun.”
“Then why did you step in?”
“Because if you died,” Shen said mildly, as though explaining the simplest fact, “the game couldn’t continue.”
Something seemed to explode in Lu’s chest.
A game.
A year of living together. Kisses. Embraces. “Come home early” every morning. Sweet-and-sour ribs. A sore shoulder needing his touch. Shen curling into his arms on rainy days.
All a game.
“Did you ever…” Lu’s voice caught. “Feel anything real for me?”
Shen looked at him.
His expression was strange. Not cruel, not triumphant. Almost curious confusion, as though the question were beyond his understanding.

“Real?” He repeated the word. “Lu Zheng, I’m a forensic physician. I’ve written your autopsy report. I know your skeletal age, your old injuries, what’s in your stomach. What do you think ‘real’ means in a relationship like that?”
He stood and went to the window.
Rain continued falling. Moisture clouded the glass.

“Have you ever wondered,” Shen said, his back to Lu, “why I could reach every scene before you? Why every analysis let me tell you precisely what came next? Why Zhou Kun, Su Wan, Old Zheng, Lin Zhinuan… all followed the lines we laid and walked straight in, one by one?”
Lu remained motionless.
Cold spread through his whole body.

“Because I arranged it,” Shen said. “I needed you to arrest them. The more you caught, the more you believed the net was closing. The closer you thought you were to the end, the less you suspected the person beside you, helping solve it.”
He turned.
The living-room light fell across his face. The same face Lu had loved for a year. But everything in the eyes had changed.
No tenderness. No shyness. No dependence.
Only a calm, appraising gaze, as though admiring a finished work.

“Nine core members.” Shen counted on his fingers. “White Rose was the scapegoat I released. Iris and Daisy grew the plants. Datura prepared the drugs. Lily of the Valley handled transport. Bauhinia did the hauling. Lin Zhinuan was the shield I pushed forward.”
He looked up.
“Eight. All gifts from me to you.”
Lu’s nails dug into his palms.
“And you?”
“I’m Black Rose,” Shen said. “The founder. From the first member to the ninth, I chose them all. From the first murder until now, I designed everything.”
He stepped closer.
“And you, Team Leader Lu…” His voice softened, almost returning to its familiar tenderness. “You are the best game I have ever played.”
In the kitchen, the pan of ribs had boiled dry.
Smoke drifted out with the burnt sweetness of the sauce. Neither man moved.
Lu looked at the person before him.
For a year, he had slept, eaten, kissed, and planned a trip to the sea beside him. He had believed he was holding someone soft, someone who needed protection.
He had been holding a blade.
“When did you begin planning all this?” Lu’s voice was hoarse.
“My first day at the bureau,” Shen said. “I saw you at my interview. You were at the far end of the corridor, banging a desk at your subordinates. I thought: that man could be useful.”
“So you deliberately joined forensics.”
“Yes. Only beside you could I know every move. Where you set surveillance at midnight, whom you planned to arrest tomorrow, how far your suspicions had reached—all of it under my eyes.”
Shen returned to the sofa and picked up the phone Lu knew so well.
Two taps lit the screen. A string of numbers appeared, with no contact name.

“The day after Zhou Kun’s arrest, I messaged the Pruner that the third piece could be sacrificed.” Shen turned the screen toward Lu. “Before Lin Zhinuan went in, I operated on her myself and implanted explosives beside her spine. She thought she was saving someone. Really, she was just another piece to discard when I was done.”
Lu looked at the screen.
The messages he watched Shen browse on the sofa every day, the exchanges he thought were conversations with friends—
All criminal instructions.
“Call the police.” Shen placed the phone on the coffee table, voice level. “I won’t run.”
Lu did not move.
“Why?”

“Because the game is over.” For the first time, something else appeared in Shen’s eyes—not emotion, but the satisfaction of completing a work. “All eight flowers have withered. Time to close the garden.”
He leaned forward slightly.

“Do you know, Lu Zheng, how tiring this year has been? Shy in the morning. Coaxing at meals. Curling into your arms at night. I have severe obsessive-compulsive disorder. I don’t even like being touched.”
He smiled faintly, cold as glass.
“When you held me, I counted your heartbeats. At one hundred and twenty, you would fall asleep.”
Lu reached toward his waist.
The holster was empty. He had locked his gun in the office safe before leaving work.
Shen watched the movement, the corner of his mouth lifting.
“Don’t bother,” he said. “Call them now. I’ll sit right here.”
Outside, the rain continued.
The smell of burning filled the room. Two place settings still waited on the table, the second one Shen had laid out that evening.
Lu took out his phone.
The screen lit. He stared at the dial pad, his finger suspended above it.
He remembered lotus-root soup. Warmth curling into his arms on rainy days. A mint-scented kiss pressed to his forehead.
All false.
He pressed three digits.
As the call connected, Shen leaned back on the sofa and closed his eyes.
Like an actor whose curtain had finally fallen.

alt.en: A rain-soaked Lu Zheng steps back from Shen Yu’an at their apartment doorway.
alt.zh: 雨中归来的陆峥在家门口避开沈予安伸来的手。

zh: 周明远正式批捕那天，下了一场秋雨。
雨从下午开始下，打在办公室窗户上噼啪响。陆峥坐在桌前，把八个人的案卷全部摊开，一张一张按顺序排好。
白玫瑰周坤。鸢尾苏晚。雏菊老郑。铃兰。紫荆。山茶林知暖。曼陀罗周明远。
八份档案，八张脸，八种花的代号。
他盯着这些名字看了整整一个下午。
技术组长进来送过一次咖啡，看见他这副样子，站在门口犹豫了一下。
"陆队，都批捕了，接下来就是检察院那边的事了。你回去休息吧。"
技术组长带上门出去了。
办公室里只剩下雨声。
陆峥站起身，走到白板前面。
白板上贴了八张照片，围成一个圈。圈的中间，他之前用红笔写了一个大大的问号。
他拿起马克笔，在那个问号旁边，写下组织的全称。
"La Rose Éternelle——永恒玫瑰。"
八个字。
他盯着这行字。
白玫瑰是周坤。鸢尾是苏晚。雏菊是老郑。铃兰。紫荆。山茶。曼陀罗。
八种花，八种植物，全部被警方连根拔起。
花园里的花开了又谢，谢了又开。
那花园的主人呢？
一个花园，不会自己长出来。总得有人播种，有人浇水，有人修剪，有人站在最高处看着一切生长。
这个人叫什么代号？
陆峥的马克笔停在白板上。
他想起林知暖在审讯室里说的那句话——"我就是你们要找的人。"
假的。她不是。她只是被推到台前的挡箭牌。
他想起周明远在审讯室里，怎么都撬不开嘴的样子。他知道上面有人，但他从来没见过那个人。
他想起老郑说的"老太太"，紫荆喊的"夫人"。这些称呼指向的，都是林知暖那个层级。
再往上呢？
再往上，还有一个人。
一个从不出现在任何通讯记录里，从不留下任何痕迹，从不和下面的人直接接触的人。
这个人怎么指挥整个组织？
陆峥的手慢慢放下来。
他转过头，目光落在窗外。雨还在下，城市被雨水模糊成一片光晕。
一个念头像冰水一样从头顶浇下来。
——这个人，根本不需要通过通讯软件指挥。
他就在市局里。
他每天和他们一起开会，一起分析案情，一起追捕自己的手下。他知道警方的每一步动作，知道每一条线索的走向，知道什么时候该抛一个替罪羊，什么时候该故意露一个破绽。
他甚至能在陆峥身边，扮演一个温柔的恋人。
陆峥的手指开始发抖。
他走到桌边，翻开沈予安的那份背景调查。
父亲早逝。母亲改嫁。从小跟着外婆长大。医科大学本硕连读。毕业进市局。
没有异常出入境。没有异常银行流水。没有可疑社会关系。
太干净了。
干净得像一份被精心打磨过的简历。
一个孤儿。一个没有根的人。一个谁都查不出过去的人。
他站在办公室中央，听着外面的雨声。
雨打在窗户上，一下一下，像心跳。
他没有回办公室收拾东西。他抓起外套就往外走。
地下车库，车子发动，轮胎碾过积水路面。雨刷开到最大，前面的路还是模糊的。
他开得很快。闯了一个黄灯，被电子眼拍了都不管。
脑子里翻来覆去只有一个画面——雕塑公园第一次见面，沈予安穿着白大褂走过来，口罩上面露出一双眼睛。
那双眼睛里，什么情绪都没有。
那时候他以为是法医见惯了尸体的冷静。
现在想来——
那是一个猎人，在观察自己的猎物。
车停在小区地下车库。
他坐在车里，没有立刻上去。雨还在下，车库顶上的灯管嗡嗡响，光线惨白。
他掏出手机，翻到沈予安的号码。
通话记录显示，今天下午五点十七分，沈予安给他发过一条消息："今晚做你爱吃的糖醋排骨，早点回来。"
陆峥盯着这条消息看了很久。
他锁了屏，下车，走进电梯。
电梯数字往上跳。十楼。十五楼。二十楼。
叮的一声。
他走出来，掏钥匙，开门。
门开了。
客厅里亮着暖黄的灯。厨房传来抽油烟机的声音，混着糖醋排骨的甜香味。
沈予安站在灶台前面，围着围裙，正在翻锅里的排骨。听见开门声，他回过头，脸上是那个熟悉的、温柔的笑。
"回来了？今天怎么这么晚。"
陆峥站在玄关，没有动。
他看着厨房里的这个人。
灯光从头顶打下来，在他头发上打出一圈浅金。围裙带子在腰后面系了个蝴蝶结。手里拿着锅铲，袖口卷到手肘，露出那截细白的手腕。
这是他住了一年的家。这是他每天抱着睡觉的人。这是他曾经发誓要保护一辈子的人。
"怎么了。"沈予安看见他站着不动，关了火，擦了擦手走过来，"身上都湿了，我给你拿毛巾。"
他走到陆峥面前，伸手想碰他的脸。
陆峥往后退了一步。
沈予安的手停在半空中。
客厅里安静下来。抽油烟机的声音已经关了，只剩下厨房锅里排骨还在滋滋响。
"陆峥？"沈予安的声音有一点疑惑。
陆峥抬起头，看着他。
"你是什么时候开始的。"
沈予安的表情没有变化。"什么什么时候。"
"组织。"陆峥的声音很稳，稳得像结了冰，"La Rose Éternelle。你从什么时候开始的。"
沈予安看着他。
两秒。
他脸上的那个温柔的表情，像面具一样，一点一点卸下来。
不是惊慌。不是被识破后的慌乱。是一种很平静的、终于等到这一刻的释然。
他收回手，转过身，走到沙发旁边坐下来。
动作很自然，像只是听完了一段普通的工作汇报。
"你什么时候知道的。"他问。
声音变了。
不是平时那个温柔的、带着一点撒娇尾音的声音。是一种更冷、更平、不带任何情绪的语调。
陆峥站在原地。
他听到这个声音的时候，心里最后那一点自欺欺人的希望，碎了。
"今天。"陆峥说，"就在办公室。"
沈予安"哦"了一声。他伸手解开围裙的带子，把围裙叠好，放在沙发扶手上。
那个动作太从容了。从容得像在自己家——他本来就是在自己家，这一年来，他每天都在演。
"八个人。"陆峥的声音发紧，"白玫瑰、鸢尾、雏菊、铃兰、紫荆、山茶、曼陀罗。八朵花，全部抓齐了。花园里所有的花都开了。"
他往前走了一步。
"就差一朵。"
沈予安抬起头，看着他。
灯光底下，他的眼睛很平静。没有恐惧，没有愧疚，没有被揭穿后的狼狈。
"黑玫瑰。"陆峥说。
两个字落地。
厨房锅里的排骨还在滋滋响，糖醋的甜味弥漫在整个客厅里。
沈予安靠在沙发上，手臂搭着扶手，姿势松弛。
"你比我想的晚了两周。"他说。
陆峥的手在身侧攥紧了。
"肩伤。"他说，"去年那个逃犯，你替我挡的那一枪。也是设计好的？"
"不是。"沈予安歪了歪头，"那个是真的。我没想到他会掏枪。"
"那你为什么挡。"
"因为如果你死了，"沈予安的语气很平淡，像在解释一个再简单不过的事实，"这个游戏就没法继续了。"
陆峥觉得有什么东西在胸腔里炸开。
游戏。
这一年的同居。接吻。拥抱。每天早上那句"早点回来"。糖醋排骨。肩膀疼了要他揉。下雨天往他怀里钻。
全部是游戏。
"你从来没有……"陆峥的声音卡了一下，"对我有过一点真的？"
沈予安看着他。
他的表情很奇怪。不是残忍，不是得意，是一种近乎好奇的困惑，像在听一个他完全无法理解的问题。
"真的？"他重复了一遍这个词，"陆峥，我是法医。你的尸检报告我都写过，你的骨龄、你的旧伤、你胃里有什么我都知道。你觉得这种关系里，'真的'是什么？"
他站起身，走到窗边。
雨还在下。窗户上蒙着一层水雾。
"你有没有想过，"沈予安的背影对着他，"为什么所有的现场，我都能比你先到？为什么每一次分析，我都能精准地告诉你下一步是什么？为什么周坤、苏晚、老郑、林知暖……一个一个，全部顺着我们布的线，自己走进来？"
陆峥站在原地。
他浑身发冷。
"因为那是我安排的。"沈予安说，"我需要你们抓他们。抓得越多，你越觉得案子在收网。你越觉得快结束了，你就越不会怀疑，那个一直站在你身边帮你破案的人。"
他转过身。
客厅的灯光打在他脸上，那张脸还是那张脸——他爱了一年的脸。但眼睛里的东西完全变了。
没有温柔。没有羞怯。没有依赖。
只有一种冷静的、审视的、像在欣赏一件作品的目光。
"九个核心成员。"沈予安伸出手，掰着手指数，"白玫瑰是我放出来的替罪羊。鸢尾和雏菊是负责种植的。曼陀罗是配药的。铃兰管运输。紫荆管搬运。林知暖是我推出去的挡箭牌。"
他抬起眼。
"八个。全部是我送给你的礼物。"
陆峥的指甲嵌进掌心。
"那你呢。"
"我是黑玫瑰。"沈予安说，"这个组织的创始人。从第一个人到第九个人，全是我挑的。从第一起命案到现在，全部是我设计的。"
他往前走了一步。
"而你，陆队长，"他的声音放轻了，像回到了平时那个温柔的语调里，"是我这一辈子玩过最好的一个游戏。"
厨房的锅里，排骨烧干了。
烟从厨房飘出来，混着糖醋的焦味。两个人都没有动。
陆峥看着眼前这个人。
这一年来，他在这个人身边睡觉，吃饭，接吻，计划着去看海。他以为自己抱住了一个柔软的、需要被保护的人。
他抱住的，是一把刀。
"你从什么时候开始计划这一切的。"陆峥的声音哑了。
"从我进市局第一天。"沈予安说，"面试的时候我就看见你了。你站在走廊那头，跟下属拍桌子。我当时想——这个人，好用。"
"所以你故意进法医室。"
"对。只有站在你身边，我才能知道你的每一步动作。你半夜在哪里布控，你明天要去抓谁，你怀疑到了哪一步——全部在我眼皮底下。"
沈予安走回沙发旁边，拿起那部陆峥再熟悉不过的手机。
他按了两下，屏幕亮了。上面是一串号码，备注是空的。
"周坤被抓的第二天，我发消息给修剪匠，告诉他第三个棋子可以抛了。"沈予安把手机转过来，让陆峥看屏幕，"林知暖进去之前，我亲自给她做的手术，把炸药植进她的脊椎旁边。她以为她在救人，其实她只是我用完就扔的一颗棋子。"
陆峥看着屏幕。
那些他每天看见沈予安在沙发上刷的消息，那些他以为是在和朋友聊天的记录——
全是犯罪指令。
"你报警吧。"沈予安把手机放在茶几上，声音很平，"我不会跑。"
陆峥没有动。
"为什么。"
"因为游戏结束了。"沈予安看着他，眼睛里第一次出现了一点别的东西——不是情绪，是一种完成了作品之后的满足，"八朵花都谢了，花园也该关门了。"
他往前倾了倾身。
"你知道吗，陆峥。这一年我演得真累。早上要害羞，吃饭要撒娇，晚上要往你怀里钻。我有严重的强迫症，我根本不喜欢别人碰我。"
他笑了一下。那个笑容很淡，冷得像玻璃。
"你抱我的时候，我数着你的心跳，数到第一百二十下的时候，你就会睡着。"
陆峥伸出手，摸向腰间。
枪套是空的。他下班的时候把枪锁在办公室保险柜里了。
沈予安看着他的动作，嘴角弯了一下。
"别找了。"他说，"你现在打电话叫人来，我就在这儿坐着。"
窗外的雨还在下。
焦糊味弥漫在客厅里。桌上还摆着两副碗筷，是沈予安晚上多摆的那副。
陆峥掏出手机。
屏幕亮了。他盯着拨号界面，手指悬在上面。
他想起那碗莲藕排骨汤。想起下雨天往他怀里钻的温度。想起那个在他额头上印下的、带着薄荷味的吻。
全部是假的。
他按下了三个数字。
电话接通的那一瞬间，沈予安靠在沙发上，闭上了眼睛。
像一个终于谢幕的演员。
en: An autumn rain fell on the day Zhou Mingyuan’s arrest was formally approved.
It began in the afternoon, pattering against the office window. Lu sat at his desk with all eight case files spread out, arranging them page by page.
White Rose, Zhou Kun. Iris, Su Wan. Daisy, Old Zheng. Lily of the Valley. Bauhinia. Camellia, Lin Zhinuan. Datura, Zhou Mingyuan.
Eight files. Eight faces. Eight flower codenames.
He stared at the names for an entire afternoon.
The technical team leader brought coffee once. Seeing him, he hesitated in the doorway.
“Team Leader Lu, the arrests have all been approved. It’s for the procuratorate now. Go home and rest.”
“Mm.”
The team leader closed the door behind him.
Only the rain remained.
Lu rose and went to the whiteboard.
Eight photographs formed a circle. In its center was the large red question mark he had drawn earlier.
He picked up the marker and wrote the organization’s full name beside it.
“La Rose Éternelle—the Eternal Rose.”
A short line of words.
He stared at it.
White Rose was Zhou Kun. Iris was Su Wan. Daisy was Old Zheng. Lily of the Valley. Bauhinia. Camellia. Datura.
Eight flowers, eight plants, all pulled up by the police.
The garden’s flowers bloomed and withered, withered and bloomed again.
What about the gardener?
A garden could not create itself. Someone had to sow, water, prune, and stand above it all, watching it grow.
What was that person’s codename?
Lu’s marker stopped against the board.
He remembered Lin Zhinuan’s words in the interview room: “I’m the person you’re looking for.”
False. She was not. Only a shield pushed to the front.
He remembered Zhou Mingyuan’s refusal to speak. He knew someone was above him, but had never met that person.
He remembered Old Zheng’s “old lady” and Bauhinia’s “Madam.” Those titles pointed to Lin Zhinuan’s level.
And above that?
Above that, there was someone else.
Someone who never appeared in any communication record, never left a trace, never dealt directly with the people below.
How did this person command the whole organization?
Lu slowly lowered his hand.
He turned toward the window. Rain blurred the city into a haze of light.
A thought washed over him like ice water.
This person did not need messaging software to direct anything.
He was inside the bureau.

Every day, he attended their meetings, analyzed their cases, and pursued his own subordinates alongside them. He knew every police move, every clue’s direction, when to offer a scapegoat, when to expose a deliberate flaw.
He could even stand beside Lu and play a gentle lover.
Lu’s fingers began to shake.
He went to the desk and opened Shen’s background report.
Father died early. Mother remarried. Raised by his grandmother. Combined undergraduate and master’s medical program. Joined the bureau after graduation.
No unusual border crossings. No unusual bank transactions. No suspicious connections.
Too clean.
As clean as a meticulously polished résumé.
An orphan. Someone without roots. Someone whose past no one could uncover.
He stood in the middle of the office, listening to the rain.
It struck the window beat by beat, like a heart.
He did not return to his office to gather his things. He seized his jacket and went out.
Down in the garage, the engine started. Tires rolled through standing water. Even with the wipers at full speed, the road ahead remained blurred.
He drove fast, running a yellow light without caring whether the camera caught him.
One image turned over and over in his mind: their first meeting at the sculpture park, Shen approaching in a white coat, only his eyes visible above the mask.
There had been no emotion in those eyes.
At the time, Lu had assumed it was a forensic physician’s familiarity with death.
Now he understood—
It was a hunter studying his prey.
He parked in the complex’s underground garage.
He remained in the car instead of going straight up. Rain still fell outside. Overhead tubes hummed, casting a sickly white light.
He took out his phone and found Shen’s number.
The call history showed a message sent at 5:17 that afternoon: “Making your favorite sweet-and-sour ribs tonight. Come home early.”
Lu stared at it for a long time.
He locked the screen, got out, and entered the elevator.
The floor numbers rose. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty.
A chime.
He stepped out, took his keys, and unlocked the door.
It opened.
Warm yellow light filled the living room. The kitchen extractor hummed over the sweet scent of ribs.
Shen stood at the stove in an apron, turning the ribs in the pan. At the sound of the door, he looked back with that familiar, gentle smile.
“You’re home? Why so late?”
Lu stood in the entrance without moving.
He looked at the person in the kitchen.
Overhead light edged Shen’s hair in pale gold. His apron was tied in a bow at the back. He held a spatula, sleeves rolled to his elbows, those slender pale wrists exposed.
This was the home Lu had lived in for a year. The person he held every night. The person he had sworn to protect for the rest of his life.
“What’s wrong?” Seeing him motionless, Shen switched off the stove, wiped his hands, and approached. “You’re soaked. I’ll get a towel.”
He came up to Lu and reached for his face.
Lu stepped back.
Shen’s hand stopped in midair.
The living room fell quiet. The extractor had stopped. Only the ribs still sizzled in the kitchen pan.
“Lu Zheng?” A little puzzlement entered Shen’s voice.
Lu raised his head and looked at him.
“When did you start?”
Shen’s expression did not change. “Start what?”
“The organization.” Lu’s voice was steady, frozen solid. “La Rose Éternelle. When did you start it?”
Shen looked at him.
Two seconds.
The gentle expression came away little by little, like a mask being removed.
No panic. No alarm at being discovered. Only a quiet release, as though this moment had finally arrived.
He lowered his hand, turned, and sat beside the sofa.
The movement was natural, as though he had merely heard an ordinary work report.
“When did you know?” he asked.
His voice had changed.
Not the familiar tenderness with its faintly coaxing inflection. This was colder, flatter, without emotion.
Lu stood where he was.
At that voice, the last self-deceiving fragment of hope inside him broke.
“Today,” Lu said. “In the office.”
“Oh.” Shen untied his apron, folded it neatly, and placed it on the sofa arm.
He was too composed. As though in his own home—which, of course, he was. Every day for the past year, he had been acting.
“Eight people.” Lu’s voice tightened. “White Rose, Iris, Daisy, Lily of the Valley, Bauhinia, Camellia, Datura. Eight flowers. All caught. Every flower in the garden has bloomed.”
He took a step forward.
“Except one.”
Shen raised his head.
Under the light, his eyes were calm. No fear, no guilt, no humiliation at being exposed.
“Black Rose,” Lu said.
The words fell between them.
The ribs still sizzled in the kitchen. Their sweet-and-sour fragrance filled the room.
Shen leaned back, an arm resting loosely on the sofa.
“You took two weeks longer than I expected,” he said.
Lu’s hand clenched at his side.
“The shoulder wound,” he said. “That fugitive last year. The bullet you took for me. Was that planned too?”
“No.” Shen tilted his head. “That was real. I didn’t expect him to draw a gun.”
“Then why did you step in?”
“Because if you died,” Shen said mildly, as though explaining the simplest fact, “the game couldn’t continue.”
Something seemed to explode in Lu’s chest.
A game.
A year of living together. Kisses. Embraces. “Come home early” every morning. Sweet-and-sour ribs. A sore shoulder needing his touch. Shen curling into his arms on rainy days.
All a game.
“Did you ever…” Lu’s voice caught. “Feel anything real for me?”
Shen looked at him.
His expression was strange. Not cruel, not triumphant. Almost curious confusion, as though the question were beyond his understanding.

“Real?” He repeated the word. “Lu Zheng, I’m a forensic physician. I’ve written your autopsy report. I know your skeletal age, your old injuries, what’s in your stomach. What do you think ‘real’ means in a relationship like that?”
He stood and went to the window.
Rain continued falling. Moisture clouded the glass.

“Have you ever wondered,” Shen said, his back to Lu, “why I could reach every scene before you? Why every analysis let me tell you precisely what came next? Why Zhou Kun, Su Wan, Old Zheng, Lin Zhinuan… all followed the lines we laid and walked straight in, one by one?”
Lu remained motionless.
Cold spread through his whole body.

“Because I arranged it,” Shen said. “I needed you to arrest them. The more you caught, the more you believed the net was closing. The closer you thought you were to the end, the less you suspected the person beside you, helping solve it.”
He turned.
The living-room light fell across his face. The same face Lu had loved for a year. But everything in the eyes had changed.
No tenderness. No shyness. No dependence.
Only a calm, appraising gaze, as though admiring a finished work.

“Nine core members.” Shen counted on his fingers. “White Rose was the scapegoat I released. Iris and Daisy grew the plants. Datura prepared the drugs. Lily of the Valley handled transport. Bauhinia did the hauling. Lin Zhinuan was the shield I pushed forward.”
He looked up.
“Eight. All gifts from me to you.”
Lu’s nails dug into his palms.
“And you?”
“I’m Black Rose,” Shen said. “The founder. From the first member to the ninth, I chose them all. From the first murder until now, I designed everything.”
He stepped closer.
“And you, Team Leader Lu…” His voice softened, almost returning to its familiar tenderness. “You are the best game I have ever played.”
In the kitchen, the pan of ribs had boiled dry.
Smoke drifted out with the burnt sweetness of the sauce. Neither man moved.
Lu looked at the person before him.
For a year, he had slept, eaten, kissed, and planned a trip to the sea beside him. He had believed he was holding someone soft, someone who needed protection.
He had been holding a blade.
“When did you begin planning all this?” Lu’s voice was hoarse.
“My first day at the bureau,” Shen said. “I saw you at my interview. You were at the far end of the corridor, banging a desk at your subordinates. I thought: that man could be useful.”
“So you deliberately joined forensics.”
“Yes. Only beside you could I know every move. Where you set surveillance at midnight, whom you planned to arrest tomorrow, how far your suspicions had reached—all of it under my eyes.”
Shen returned to the sofa and picked up the phone Lu knew so well.
Two taps lit the screen. A string of numbers appeared, with no contact name.

“The day after Zhou Kun’s arrest, I messaged the Pruner that the third piece could be sacrificed.” Shen turned the screen toward Lu. “Before Lin Zhinuan went in, I operated on her myself and implanted explosives beside her spine. She thought she was saving someone. Really, she was just another piece to discard when I was done.”
Lu looked at the screen.
The messages he watched Shen browse on the sofa every day, the exchanges he thought were conversations with friends—
All criminal instructions.
“Call the police.” Shen placed the phone on the coffee table, voice level. “I won’t run.”
Lu did not move.
“Why?”

“Because the game is over.” For the first time, something else appeared in Shen’s eyes—not emotion, but the satisfaction of completing a work. “All eight flowers have withered. Time to close the garden.”
He leaned forward slightly.

“Do you know, Lu Zheng, how tiring this year has been? Shy in the morning. Coaxing at meals. Curling into your arms at night. I have severe obsessive-compulsive disorder. I don’t even like being touched.”
He smiled faintly, cold as glass.
“When you held me, I counted your heartbeats. At one hundred and twenty, you would fall asleep.”
Lu reached toward his waist.
The holster was empty. He had locked his gun in the office safe before leaving work.
Shen watched the movement, the corner of his mouth lifting.
“Don’t bother,” he said. “Call them now. I’ll sit right here.”
Outside, the rain continued.
The smell of burning filled the room. Two place settings still waited on the table, the second one Shen had laid out that evening.
Lu took out his phone.
The screen lit. He stared at the dial pad, his finger suspended above it.
He remembered lotus-root soup. Warmth curling into his arms on rainy days. A mint-scented kiss pressed to his forehead.
All false.
He pressed three digits.
As the call connected, Shen leaned back on the sofa and closed his eyes.
Like an actor whose curtain had finally fallen.

alt.en: Lu Zheng makes the call while Shen Yu’an sits calmly beside a folded apron.
alt.zh: 陆峥拨出电话，沈予安平静坐在折好的围裙旁。

zh: 电话拨出去，响了三声被接起来。
"队里。"
"我是陆峥。"他的声音稳得不像话，"马上带人到我家。地址我发你。多带枪。"
电话那头愣了一下。"陆队？出什么事了？"
"来了再说。"
他挂了电话，把手机放在茶几上。
沈予安靠在沙发上，手臂搭着扶手，表情平静得像在看一场和自己无关的戏。他甚至偏过头，看了一眼厨房里还在冒烟的锅。
"排骨要糊了。"他说。
陆峥没理他。
二十分钟后，楼下传来急刹车的声音。
楼梯间里响起杂乱的脚步声，由远及近。技术组长拍门的声音很响，一边拍一边喊："陆队！陆队你在里面吗！"
沈予安从沙发上站起来。
他举起双手，动作很慢，像一个配合警方调查的普通市民。
"开门吧。"他对陆峥说，"我不跑。"
陆峥走过去，拉开门。
外面站着五六个队员，全部穿防弹衣，手里端着枪。技术组长看见陆峥站在门口，脸色发白，立刻冲进来。
"陆队！怎么回事？你打电话那声音——"
"里面。"陆峥偏过头。
技术组长顺着他的目光看过去。
沈予安站在客厅中央，双手举着，姿态配合。他穿那件浅灰色家居服，头发松松的，看上去和平时没有任何区别。
"沈法医？"技术组长愣住了，"你怎么在这？"
"他是黑玫瑰。"陆峥说。
客厅里安静了一秒。
队员们面面相觑。技术组长皱着眉，枪口下意识往沈予安方向偏了偏。
"陆队，你是不是……"
"铐上。"陆峥的声音很硬。
两个队员上前，一左一右架住沈予安的手臂。冰凉的金属手铐咔哒一声扣在他手腕上。
沈予安没有反抗。他甚至笑了一下，那个笑容很淡，带着一种"终于演完了"的轻松。
"走吧。"他说。
两个队员一左一右押着他往门口走。
经过陆峥身边的时候，沈予安偏过头，看了他一眼。
那一眼很短。短到旁边的队员都没注意到。
但陆峥看见了。
那双眼睛里没有任何情绪。没有被抓的狼狈，没有对陆峥的怨怼，没有恋人之间的不舍。
只有一种冷冰冰的、像在打量一件工具的目光。
就在这时。
沈予安动了。
他的身体猛地往下一沉，肩膀撞开左边那个队员的胸口。同时手腕一翻——不知道什么时候，他手腕上的手铐已经开了，钥匙藏在指缝里。他反手夺过右边那个队员腰间的配枪，动作快得像一道影子。
下一秒，枪口抵在了那个队员的太阳穴上。
"都别动。"
声音很平。
整个客厅的空气凝固了。
其他队员齐刷刷举枪，对准沈予安。被枪指着太阳穴的那个队员僵在原地，额头的汗一下子冒出来。
"沈予安！你干什么！"技术组长吼。
"闭嘴。"
沈予安的手稳稳地扣着扳机。他的视线越过枪口，落在陆峥脸上。
"我跟你说过，"他说，"游戏结束了。"
就在这时——
卧室的门开了。
阳台的推拉门开了。
储藏室的小门开了。
三个方向，六个人影从不同的房间里走出来。全部穿黑色作战服，手里端着微冲，动作利落得像训练过几百遍。他们散开站位，枪口齐刷刷对准客厅里的警察。
两个从卧室出来的男人，一个高一个矮。高的那个戴眼镜，陆峥觉得有点眼熟——像在哪里见过。矮的那个下巴上有一道疤，眼神阴鸷。
阳台上走出来一个女人，三十岁上下，短发，手里拎着一把短管霰弹枪。
储藏室里出来两个人，一男一女，都是二十七八岁的样子。
最后一个人从厨房门后面绕出来，手里端着枪，懒洋洋地靠在门框上。
八个人。
八个陆峥从来没见过的人。
技术组长的脸白了。"你们……你们是谁？"
沈予安笑了。
他枪口还抵着那个队员的太阳穴，偏过头，像在介绍什么稀松平常的事情。
"介绍一下。"他说，"白玫瑰。鸢尾。雏菊。铃兰。紫荆。山茶。曼陀罗。"
他每说一个名字，那些人里就有一个人微微颔首。
"你之前抓的那些，"沈予安的目光回到陆峥脸上，"都是替身。周坤是个赌鬼，我给了他家里一笔钱，让他替我进去坐十年。苏晚是个欠债的，我帮她还了三百万。老郑的孙女有白血病，我出的手术费。"
他顿了顿。
"他们以为自己在替家人换一条命。其实他们只是我放在监狱里的稻草人。"
陆峥的拳头在身侧攥紧。
那些他熬了无数个夜抓回来的人。那些他以为是正义得到伸张的罪犯。
全是假的。
"好了。"沈予安偏了偏头，"叙旧就到这。"
他用枪柄砸在被挟持那个队员的后颈上。那人闷哼一声，软倒在地。
八个人同时后退，往窗边移动。
短发女人端着霰弹枪，一枪托砸碎了阳台的落地玻璃窗。玻璃碎片哗啦啦掉了一地，夜风灌进来，带着雨水的味道。
远处传来直升机的轰鸣声。
由远及近。
"都站在原地。"沈予安退到窗边，枪口还对着屋里的人，"谁动一下，我开枪。"
队员们僵在原地。技术组长的枪举着，手在抖。
沈予安最后看了陆峥一眼。
"对了。"他像想起什么，从家居服口袋里掏出一个黑色遥控器，举起来晃了晃。
"这栋楼，从一楼到顶楼，我装了四十斤C4。"他说，"遥控器在我手里。你们现在追，或者拆弹，或者做任何一件让我不高兴的事——"
他用大拇指顶了一下遥控器的开关。
"整栋楼的人，陪你们一起走。"
陆峥的眼睛红了。
不是气的。是那种从骨头里涌上来的、被人从里到外耍了一年的荒谬感。他张了张嘴，一个字都说不出来。
沈予安看着他。
然后他笑了。
那个笑容很轻。没有得意，没有嘲讽，甚至没有恶意。就是一种演员谢幕时，对最后一排观众的、礼貌的微笑。
他转身，跨上窗台。
直升机已经悬停在阳台外面。软梯垂下来，在夜风里晃。
八个成员一个接一个翻出去，抓住软梯往上爬。沈予安最后一个。他翻上窗台的时候，回头看了一眼。
陆峥站在客厅中央。
雨水从破碎的阳台灌进来，打湿了他的裤脚。他的眼睛盯着沈予安，瞳孔收缩，嘴唇抿成一条线。
那里面有愤怒，有震惊，有被背叛之后的痛。
沈予安看着他，看了两秒。
然后他抬起手，对着陆峥，按了一下那个遥控器。
陆峥的瞳孔猛地放大。
他看见那个动作，看见沈予安的拇指按下去，看见遥控器上的红灯闪了一下。
——炸弹要炸了。
整个世界在那一秒停住了。
技术组长吼了一句什么。旁边有队员往门口冲。
但沈予安只是站在窗台上，对着陆峥，很慢地、一个字一个字地，用口型说：
然后他歪了歪头，补了后半句：
他翻出了窗台。
直升机爬高，旋翼把雨水搅成一片白雾。沈予安坐在舱门口，两条腿悬在外面。他从旁边一个成员手里接过一个东西——一个便携小火锅，还有一副扑克牌。
那个成员笑了一声，用粤语说了句什么。
沈予安拆开火锅盖子，热气冒出来。他往锅里下了一片肥牛，动作慢悠悠的。
下面，那栋楼还在。
没有爆炸。
红灯闪了一下就灭了。四十斤C4是真的，但他从来没打算在这里炸。这栋楼是他选的，是他和陆峥住了一年的地方，炸了多可惜。
他只是想看看，陆峥听见"炸弹"两个字的时候，脸上是什么表情。
现在他看到了。
沈予安端着小火锅，往下看了最后一眼。
陆峥站在破碎的阳台上，雨水打湿了他的头发，贴在额头上。他仰着头，眼睛死死盯着直升机的方向。
两个人隔着五十米的高空，对视了一秒。
沈予安举起手里的小火锅，像在敬酒。
然后他转过身，钻进机舱。
舱门关上。
直升机调转机头，消失在雨夜的云层里。
阳台上，只剩下雨声。
技术组长跑过来，一把抓住陆峥的胳膊。"陆队！陆你没事吧？拆弹组马上到！四十斤C4，我们得马上——"
陆峥站着没动。
他的眼睛还盯着直升机消失的方向。
雨水顺着他的脸颊往下淌，分不清是雨还是别的什么。
他的手在抖。
不是怕的。
是因为他终于想明白了一件事——
这一年里，沈予安在他怀里撒娇的时候，在他额头上印下吻的时候，在下雨天往他脖子里钻，一年相处的回忆跟针一样狠狠扎进脑袋刺的生疼
而他说的最后那句话。
"游戏还没真正的结束呢。"
什么游戏？
陆峥站在破碎的阳台上，听着雨声，看着黑沉沉的夜空。
他知道，这只是开始。
那个人，还会回来。
下一次见面，就不是恋人了。
——End                                   （可能会有第二季）

作者有话要说：写这篇小说，我从来不是为了推崇犯罪，更不是教大家去学坏、模仿恶劣行为。文中所有的黑暗剧情、反派的极端做法以及反社会人格的设定，全都只是用来当反面教材的。我写这些内容，唯一的目的是提醒大家，而不是美化罪恶、宣扬恶行。老话讲，人不可貌相，海水不可斗量。现实生活真的没有我们想象中那么单纯，很多心思阴暗、藏着坏念头的人，就潜藏在我们身边。他们外表看着温和、待人友善，会刻意展露一点点善意，可这并不代表他们本性就是好人。很多人就是太容易相信表象，看到别人一点好，就彻底放下戒备，毫无保留地去信任对方。不管是交朋友，还是谈恋爱，真诚待人没错，但绝对不能傻乎乎地全盘交付。自古有言，害人之心不可有，防人之心不可无。我们可以保持善良，但一定要给自己留底线、留防备。文中写的这个偏执疯狂、极端冷血的反派，虽然是经过艺术放大的角色，但绝对不是凭空虚构的。现实里，性格扭曲、心态极端、思想阴暗的人一点都不少，只是大多没有剧情里这么夸张、没有做出这么极端的坏事而已。我写下这些黑暗的剧情，就是想给所有人提个醒：人心复杂，善恶难分。希望大家在日常生活里，多留一个心眼，保持一份清醒，不要被表面的温柔和善意蒙骗，更不要轻易相信一个人的全部。千万不要因为单纯和心软，让自己变成被伤害、被算计的受害者。最后再郑重说一次：本文所有的犯罪情节、极端行为和黑暗设定，都只是剧情创作，仅作反面警示用途。我本人坚决反对一切违法犯罪行为，绝不崇尚、也绝不教唆任何恶劣行径。请各位读者理性看文，切勿模仿剧情、不要对号入座，好好生活，谨慎识人，好好保护自己。
en: The call rang three times before someone answered.
“Team office.”
“This is Lu Zheng.” His voice was unnaturally steady. “Bring officers to my home immediately. I’ll send the address. Bring extra firearms.”
A hesitation at the other end. “Team Leader Lu? What happened?”
“I’ll explain when you get here.”
He ended the call and placed the phone on the coffee table.
Shen leaned against the sofa, an arm on the armrest, as calm as though watching a play that had nothing to do with him. He even glanced toward the smoking pan in the kitchen.
“The ribs are burning,” he said.
Lu ignored him.
Twenty minutes later, brakes screeched below.
Disordered footsteps approached through the stairwell. The technical team leader pounded on the door, shouting, “Team Leader Lu! Are you in there?”
Shen rose from the sofa.
He lifted both hands slowly, like an ordinary citizen cooperating with an investigation.
“Open it,” he told Lu. “I’m not running.”
Lu went over and opened the door.
Five or six officers waited outside, all in bulletproof vests, guns ready. At the sight of Lu’s pale face, the technical team leader rushed in.
“Team Leader Lu! What happened? Your voice on the phone—”
“Inside.” Lu turned his head.
The team leader followed his gaze.
Shen stood in the middle of the living room with his hands raised, perfectly cooperative. Pale-gray loungewear, loose hair. He looked no different from usual.
“Dr. Shen?” The team leader froze. “What are you doing here?”
“He’s Black Rose,” Lu said.
The living room fell silent for a second.
The officers exchanged looks. Frowning, the technical team leader instinctively shifted his muzzle toward Shen.
“Team Leader Lu, are you…”
“Cuff him.” Lu’s voice was hard.
Two officers stepped forward and took his arms. Cold metal clicked shut around his wrists.
Shen did not resist. He even smiled faintly, with the relief of someone whose performance was finally over.
“Let’s go,” he said.
The officers escorted him toward the door.
As he passed Lu, Shen turned his head and looked at him.
The glance was brief. Too brief for the officers beside him to notice.
But Lu saw it.
No emotion in those eyes. No humiliation at arrest, no resentment toward Lu, no lover’s reluctance to part.
Only a cold appraisal, as though examining a tool.
Then—
Shen moved.

He dropped his weight abruptly, his shoulder striking the officer on his left in the chest. At the same time, he turned his wrist. Somehow the cuffs were already open, a key hidden between his fingers. He reached back and seized the other officer’s sidearm, moving like a shadow.
A moment later, the muzzle pressed against that officer’s temple.
“Nobody move.”
His voice was flat.
The air in the room seemed to solidify.
The other officers raised their guns together, aiming at Shen. The hostage froze, sweat breaking across his forehead.
“Shen Yu’an! What are you doing?” the technical team leader shouted.
“Shut up.”
Shen’s hand remained steady on the trigger. His gaze passed over the gun and settled on Lu.
“I told you,” he said. “The game is over.”
At that moment—
The bedroom door opened.
The balcony’s sliding door opened.
The small storage-room door opened.

From three directions, six figures emerged, all in black tactical clothing, carrying compact submachine guns. Their movements were crisp, as though rehearsed hundreds of times. They spread out, muzzles trained on the officers in the living room.
Two men came from the bedroom, one tall, one short. The taller wore glasses and looked vaguely familiar to Lu. The shorter had a scar on his chin and a hard, menacing gaze.
A woman of about thirty emerged from the balcony, short-haired, carrying a short-barreled shotgun.
Two people came from the storage room, a man and a woman, both around twenty-seven or twenty-eight.
The last stepped from behind the kitchen door with a gun and leaned lazily against the frame.
Eight people.
Eight people Lu had never seen before.
The technical team leader went white. “Who… who are you?”
Shen smiled.
Still holding the muzzle to the officer’s temple, he tilted his head as though making an entirely ordinary introduction.
“Allow me,” he said. “White Rose. Iris. Daisy. Lily of the Valley. Bauhinia. Camellia. Datura.”
With each name, someone gave a slight nod.

“The people you arrested…” Shen looked back at Lu. “Stand-ins. Zhou Kun was a gambler. I paid his family, and he agreed to serve ten years for me. Su Wan was in debt. I paid off three million yuan. Old Zheng’s granddaughter had leukemia. I paid for her operation.”
He paused.
“They thought they were buying a life for their families. Really, they were scarecrows I placed in prison.”
Lu’s fists tightened at his sides.
The people he had stayed awake countless nights to catch. The criminals whose arrests he had believed were justice.
All false.
“All right.” Shen tilted his head. “Enough reminiscing.”
He struck the hostage at the back of the neck with the gun’s grip. The man gave a muffled cry and collapsed.
All eight retreated together toward the window.
The short-haired woman smashed the balcony’s floor-to-ceiling glass with her shotgun stock. Fragments crashed across the floor. Night wind rushed in, smelling of rain.
A helicopter’s roar sounded in the distance.
Closer and closer.
“Stay where you are.” Shen backed toward the window, still aiming into the room. “Anyone moves, I shoot.”
The officers stood rigid. The technical team leader kept his gun raised, his hands shaking.
Shen looked at Lu one last time.
“Oh, one more thing.” As though remembering something, he took a black remote from his pocket and held it up.
“This building, from the ground floor to the top—I’ve planted twenty kilos of C4,” he said. “I have the remote. Chase us, try to disarm it, or do anything else I don’t like—”
His thumb touched the switch.
“Everyone in the building goes with you.”
Lu’s eyes reddened.
Not from anger. From the absurdity rising out of his bones, the knowledge that someone had played him inside and out for a year. He opened his mouth but could not speak.
Shen watched him.
Then he smiled.
A small smile. No triumph, no mockery, not even malice. Merely an actor’s courteous smile toward the audience in the last row at the curtain call.
He turned and stepped onto the sill.
The helicopter hovered outside the balcony. A rope ladder swung in the night wind.
The eight members climbed out one after another and ascended. Shen went last. As he reached the sill, he looked back.
Lu stood in the middle of the living room.
Rain blew through the shattered balcony and soaked his trouser cuffs. His eyes remained fixed on Shen, pupils contracted, lips pressed into a line.
There was anger in them, shock, and the pain of betrayal.
Shen watched him for two seconds.
Then he lifted the remote toward Lu and pressed it.
Lu’s pupils widened sharply.
He saw the movement, saw Shen’s thumb descend, saw the remote’s red light flash.
The bomb was about to go off.
For that second, the whole world stopped.
The technical team leader shouted something. An officer nearby rushed toward the door.
But Shen simply stood on the sill and slowly, deliberately mouthed to Lu:
“The. Game. Is. Over.”
Then he tilted his head and added:
“The. Mission. Is. Not.”
He climbed out.

The helicopter rose, its rotors churning rain into white mist. Shen sat in the open doorway, legs dangling. He accepted something from another member: a portable mini hotpot and a deck of playing cards.
The member laughed and said something in Cantonese.
Shen removed the hotpot lid. Steam rose. Unhurriedly, he put in a slice of marbled beef.
Below, the building still stood.
No explosion.

The red light had flashed and gone out. The twenty kilos of C4 were real, but he had never intended to detonate them here. He had chosen this building. He and Lu had lived in it for a year. Blowing it up would have been a pity.
He had only wanted to see Lu’s expression at the word “bomb.”
Now he had.
Holding the little hotpot, Shen looked down one final time.
Lu stood on the shattered balcony, rain plastering his hair to his forehead. His head was raised, eyes fixed on the helicopter.
Across fifty meters of open air, their eyes met for one second.
Shen raised the hotpot as though offering a toast.
Then he turned and climbed into the cabin.
The door closed.
The helicopter turned away and vanished into the rainy clouds.
Only the rain remained on the balcony.
The technical team leader ran over and seized Lu’s arm. “Team Leader Lu! Lu, are you all right? Bomb disposal is on its way! Twenty kilos of C4—we have to—”
Lu did not move.
His eyes remained on the place where the helicopter had disappeared.
Water ran down his cheeks. Rain, or something else—it was impossible to tell.
His hands shook.
Not with fear.
Because at last he understood something—
All the times Shen had coaxed him from the shelter of his arms, kissed his forehead, or nestled against his neck on rainy days: a year of memories drove into his mind like needles, sharp with pain.
And those final words.
“The game isn’t truly over yet.”
What game?
Lu stood on the shattered balcony, listening to the rain, looking into the black sky.
He knew this was only the beginning.
That man would return.
The next time they met, they would no longer be lovers.
—End. (There may be a second season.)

Author’s note: I never wrote this novel to promote crime, teach anyone to do wrong, or encourage imitation of harmful behavior. Every dark plotline, extreme act by the villain, and element of the antisocial-personality characterization is intended as a negative example. My only purpose in writing these things is to remind readers to be careful, not to glamorize evil or celebrate wrongdoing. As the old saying goes, you cannot judge a person by appearance, just as you cannot measure the sea with a bucket. Real life is not as simple as we imagine. People with dark intentions may be hidden among us. They can appear gentle and friendly, deliberately displaying small acts of kindness, but that does not prove they are good at heart. Many people trust appearances too easily: they see a little goodness, lower their guard completely, and place unreserved trust in someone. Whether in friendship or romance, sincerity is right, but blindly giving everything of yourself is not. Another old saying advises us never to intend harm, yet never to abandon caution. We can remain kind while keeping boundaries and protecting ourselves. The obsessive, unhinged, extremely cold-blooded villain in this story is artistically exaggerated, but the character is not conceived from nothing. People with distorted outlooks, extreme attitudes, and dark thoughts exist in reality, even if most are less dramatic than those in fiction and do not commit such extreme crimes. I wrote these dark scenes to offer a reminder: human motives are complicated, and good and evil are not always easy to distinguish. I hope readers will remain attentive and clear-minded in daily life, avoid being deceived by surface gentleness and kindness, and not place absolute trust in someone too readily. Do not let innocence or a soft heart make you a victim of harm or manipulation. Finally, let me state this solemnly once more: all criminal plots, extreme actions, and dark settings here belong to a fictional story and serve only as cautionary examples. I firmly oppose all illegal and criminal behavior. I neither admire nor encourage wrongdoing of any kind. Please read with judgment, do not imitate the plot or identify real people with its characters, live well, be careful in judging others, and protect yourselves.

alt.en: Lu Zheng watches a helicopter vanish into the rain from the shattered balcony.
alt.zh: 陆峥站在破碎阳台上，看直升机消失于雨夜。
